title: Two Sum
insight: Each value only needs its complement looked up once. Storing values you have already passed turns the inner search into an O(1) lookup instead of a rescan.
steps: Create an empty dict mapping value to the index where you saw it.
Scan nums once with index i and value v.
Compute need = target - v; if need is already a key, return [dict[need], i].
Otherwise store dict[v] = i; checking before storing is what stops an element pairing with itself.
Exactly one answer is guaranteed, so the loop always returns before it ends.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n)
pitfall: Inserting the current value before checking for its complement, which lets one element pair with itself when target is twice that value.
bruteForce: Test every pair with two nested loops, O(n^2) time and O(1) space.

title: Add Two Numbers
insight: The lists are already least significant digit first, so one left to right pass adds aligned digits and the carry propagates naturally, with no reversal anywhere.
steps: Make a dummy head node, a tail pointer at it, and carry = 0.
Loop while either list still has a node or carry is nonzero.
Sum the two current digits, using 0 when a list is exhausted, plus carry.
Append a node holding sum % 10, set carry = sum // 10, advance each non-null pointer.
Return dummy.next, which already carries the extra leading digit if one was produced.
complexity: Time O(max(m,n)), space O(max(m,n)) output
pitfall: Ending the loop as soon as both lists end and dropping a final carry, so 5 plus 5 returns 0 instead of 10.
bruteForce: Convert both lists to integers, add, rebuild the list; overflows at the 100 digit limit.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
insight: The window never needs to shrink past the previous occurrence of the current character, so the left edge can jump straight there and the whole scan stays one pass.
steps: Keep a dict last[ch] = most recent index of ch, plus left = 0 and best = 0.
Scan right from 0 to n-1 with ch = s[right].
If ch is in last and last[ch] >= left, set left = last[ch] + 1.
Set last[ch] = right, then best = max(best, right - left + 1).
Return best; an empty string skips the loop and returns 0.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(min(n, alphabet))
pitfall: Omitting the last[ch] >= left guard, so a stale occurrence outside the window drags left backwards and inflates the answer.
bruteForce: Check every substring for uniqueness with a set, O(n^2) time at best.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
pattern: Binary search on the split point
insight: You only need a partition where every left element is at most every right element. Binary search that cut in the shorter array and derive the other cut from the total count.
steps: Swap so A is the shorter array; m = len(A), n = len(B), half = (m + n + 1) // 2.
Binary search i in [0, m] as A's cut and set j = half - i as B's cut.
Use sentinels: a left value is -inf when its cut is 0, a right value +inf when the cut is at the end.
If A[i-1] > B[j] search lower (hi = i-1); if B[j-1] > A[i] search higher (lo = i+1); else the cut is valid.
If m + n is odd return the max of the two left values, else the average of max left and min right.
complexity: Time O(log min(m,n)), space O(1)
pitfall: Binary searching the longer array, so j can fall outside B, or dropping the infinity sentinels at the boundaries.
bruteForce: Merge both arrays and index the middle, O(m+n) time and O(m+n) space.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
insight: Every palindrome has a center, and there are only 2n-1 of them: n single characters and n-1 gaps between characters. Expanding from each covers all palindromes.
steps: Track bestStart and bestLen, seeded with the first character (length 1).
For each index i, expand two pointers outward from (i, i) while the characters match.
Expand again from (i, i+1) to cover even length palindromes.
Each expansion yields a length L; if L > bestLen, set bestStart = i - (L - 1) // 2.
Return s[bestStart : bestStart + bestLen].
complexity: Time O(n^2), space O(1)
pitfall: Only expanding odd centers, which misses even palindromes such as abba, or computing the start index off by one.
bruteForce: Check all O(n^2) substrings for palindromicity, O(n^3) total.

title: Reverse Integer
insight: You cannot build the reversed number and then test it, because the build itself overflows. Test before every multiply against the 32-bit limit divided by ten.
steps: Record the sign and work with magnitudes; note that negating INT_MIN overflows in fixed width languages.
Loop while x is nonzero: take d = x % 10 then x //= 10.
Before res = res * 10 + d, return 0 if res > 214748364, or res == 214748364 and d > 7.
The same bound is safe for negatives: no valid input reverses to exactly 2147483648.
Return sign * res; a trailing zero input digit simply vanishes, which is correct.
complexity: Time O(log x), space O(1)
pitfall: Checking for overflow after the multiply, which has already wrapped or is undefined in 32-bit languages.
bruteForce: Reverse the decimal string and parse into a 64-bit type, which the problem forbids.

title: String to Integer (atoi)
insight: The grammar is strictly ordered: leading spaces, one optional sign, then digits, stopping at the first non digit. Clamp during the build, never after it.
steps: Skip leading space characters only, then read at most one + or - as the sign.
Read digits while the character is 0 to 9, building res = res * 10 + d.
Before each step clamp: if res would pass 2147483647, return INT_MAX or INT_MIN by sign.
Stop at the first non digit; trailing junk is ignored rather than an error.
Return 0 if no digit was read at all, including for an empty or sign-only string.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Skipping every whitespace kind, or accepting a sign that comes after digits; only leading spaces and one leading sign are legal.
bruteForce: Hand the digit run to a library parser and clamp after; the statement bans that, and it overflows on 200 digits.

title: Regular Expression Matching
insight: A star gives exactly two choices at each cell: drop the char-star pair entirely (zero copies), or consume one text character and stay at the same pattern position.
steps: Let dp[i][j] mean s[i:] fully matches p[j:]; table size (n+1) by (m+1) with dp[n][m] = true.
Fill i from n down to 0 and j from m-1 down to 0.
Let first = i < n and (p[j] == s[i] or p[j] == '.').
If j+1 < m and p[j+1] == '*': dp[i][j] = dp[i][j+2] or (first and dp[i+1][j]).
Else dp[i][j] = first and dp[i+1][j+1]; the answer is dp[0][0] (full match, not prefix).
complexity: Time O(n*m), space O(n*m)
pitfall: Treating star greedily or as matching exactly one character; it binds to the preceding character and may match zero copies.
bruteForce: Recurse over every star branch with no memo, exponential in the pattern length.

title: Container With Most Water
insight: Area is capped by the shorter wall, so keeping the shorter wall and moving the taller one can never improve things. Discarding the shorter wall loses no optimal pair.
steps: Set l = 0, r = n-1, best = 0.
While l < r, compute area = (r - l) * min(h[l], h[r]) and update best.
Advance l if h[l] < h[r], otherwise retreat r.
On a tie either move is safe, since every pair using that wall is already dominated.
Return best once the pointers meet.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Moving the taller wall inward, or using the count of bars between the walls as the width instead of the index distance.
bruteForce: Try every pair of walls with nested loops, O(n^2).

title: 3Sum
insight: Sorting collapses the inner search to a two pointer sweep and puts equal values side by side, so duplicate triplets are skipped by comparing neighbours rather than hashing results.
steps: Sort nums; loop i from 0 to n-3 and break once nums[i] > 0.
Skip this i when i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1], to avoid a repeated first element.
Two pointers l = i+1 and r = n-1 hunting for sum == -nums[i].
On a hit record the triplet, then advance l and retreat r past all values equal to the ones just used.
If the sum is too small move l up, if too large move r down; return the collected triplets.
complexity: Time O(n^2), space O(1) ignoring output
pitfall: Deduping with a set of tuples instead of skipping equal neighbours, or forgetting to skip duplicates right after recording a hit.
bruteForce: Three nested loops over all triples plus a set to dedupe, O(n^3).

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
insight: The digits define a fixed depth tree: level k branches over the letters of digit k, so one depth-first walk emits every combination exactly once with no dedupe needed.
steps: Store the keypad map for digits 2 through 9; 7 is pqrs and 9 is wxyz, four letters each.
Constraints give 1 to 4 digits, but return [] for an empty string since older judges test it.
Recurse with an index and a buffer of letters chosen so far.
When index == len(digits), append the joined buffer to the results.
Otherwise loop the letters of digits[index]: push, recurse at index+1, pop.
complexity: Time O(4^n * n) for n digits, space O(n) stack
pitfall: Deriving letters arithmetically as three per digit, which breaks because 7 and 9 carry four letters and shift every later digit.
bruteForce: The same enumeration via nested loops, which cannot handle a variable digit count.

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
pattern: Two pointers with a fixed gap
insight: Open a gap of n nodes between two pointers and the trailing one stops on the node just before the target when the lead reaches the end, so no length pass is needed.
steps: Create a dummy node pointing at head so deleting the head needs no special case.
Set fast = dummy and advance it n times.
Set slow = dummy, then advance both one step at a time while fast.next is not null.
slow.next is now the node to drop, so set slow.next = slow.next.next.
Return dummy.next, which is null when the one-node list was removed.
complexity: Time O(L) in one pass, space O(1)
pitfall: Skipping the dummy head, so removing the first node (n equal to the length) needs its own branch and usually crashes.
bruteForce: Count the length, then walk L-n nodes again; still O(L) but two passes and more off by one risk.

title: Valid Parentheses
insight: Brackets must close in last opened first closed order, which is exactly a stack. A closer is only ever valid against the most recent unmatched opener.
steps: Keep a map from each closer to its matching opener, plus an empty stack.
Scan the string one character at a time.
Push every opener onto the stack.
On a closer, return false if the stack is empty or its top is not the matching opener; otherwise pop.
Return true only if the stack is empty when the scan finishes.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n)
pitfall: Omitting the final empty-stack check, so a string of only openers passes, or popping an empty stack on a leading closer.
bruteForce: Repeatedly delete adjacent matching pairs until nothing changes, O(n^2).

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
insight: Relinking nodes instead of copying keeps extra space at O(1), and once one list runs dry the remainder of the other is already sorted and can be attached whole.
steps: Create a dummy node with a tail pointer sitting on it.
While both lists are non-null, attach the node with the smaller value and advance that list.
Move tail onto the node just attached.
Once the loop exits, attach whichever list still has nodes (possibly neither).
Return dummy.next, which is null when both inputs were empty.
complexity: Time O(m+n), space O(1)
pitfall: Allocating new nodes and copying values instead of splicing, or advancing both lists on a tie and losing a node.
bruteForce: Collect every value, sort, and rebuild a list, O((m+n) log(m+n)).

title: Generate Parentheses
insight: A prefix stays valid exactly while closers never exceed openers and openers never exceed n, so two counters prune the tree instead of validating finished strings.
steps: Recurse carrying the current buffer plus open and close counts.
When the buffer length is 2n, record the string and return.
If open < n, append ( and recurse with open+1.
If close < open, append ) and recurse with close+1.
Undo the append after each branch; return the collected list.
complexity: Time O(4^n / sqrt(n)) Catalan many, space O(n) depth
pitfall: Guarding the closer with close < n rather than close < open, which emits invalid strings such as )( before any check.
bruteForce: Generate all 2^(2n) bracket strings and filter the valid ones.

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
insight: Only the k current heads can hold the next smallest value, so a heap of size k produces each output node in log k time instead of rescanning all k lists.
steps: Push (value, list index, node) for every non-empty head into a min-heap.
Carry the list index as a tiebreaker so two equal values never compare the node objects.
Pop the smallest and attach that node to the tail of a dummy-headed result.
If the popped node has a next, push that next node with the same tiebreaker scheme.
Repeat until the heap empties and return dummy.next, null when every list was empty.
complexity: Time O(N log k) for N total nodes, space O(k)
pitfall: Pushing bare nodes into the heap, which throws when two values tie and the comparator falls through to the node itself.
bruteForce: Concatenate all values and sort, O(N log N), or merge lists one by one at O(N*k).

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
pattern: Block reversal after a length check
insight: Reverse a block only once you have confirmed k nodes remain, and remember the block's old head becomes its tail, which must then be wired to the next block.
steps: Use a dummy node; keep groupPrev on the node just before the current block.
Walk k steps from groupPrev to find kth; if you hit null, stop and return dummy.next unchanged.
Save groupNext = kth.next, then reverse the k nodes so each points to its predecessor.
Save oldHead = groupPrev.next, set groupPrev.next = kth, and set oldHead.next = groupNext.
Move groupPrev to oldHead and repeat for the next block.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Reversing before confirming a full group of k remains, which leaves a trailing partial group reversed instead of untouched.
bruteForce: Push the nodes into an array and relink each k block from it: O(n) space, and rewriting node values is banned.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
pattern: Binary search on the sorted half
insight: At any midpoint at least one half is fully sorted. Compare the target against that half's known range and you always know which side to discard.
steps: Set lo = 0 and hi = n-1; loop while lo <= hi with mid = (lo + hi) // 2.
Return mid when nums[mid] == target.
If nums[lo] <= nums[mid] the left half is sorted: go left when nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid], else right.
Otherwise the right half is sorted: go right when nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi], else left.
Return -1 after the loop; values are distinct, so no equal-value tie handling is needed.
complexity: Time O(log n), space O(1)
pitfall: Writing nums[lo] < nums[mid] instead of <=, which mishandles two element windows where lo equals mid.
bruteForce: Linear scan for the target, O(n), ignoring the sortedness entirely.

title: Valid Sudoku
insight: Only filled cells matter and the board need not be solvable. One pass can test each digit against its row, its column and its 3x3 box at the same time.
steps: Keep 9 row sets, 9 column sets and 9 box sets, or one set of tagged strings.
Scan all 81 cells, skipping any cell holding a dot.
Compute the box index as (r // 3) * 3 + (c // 3).
Return false if that digit is already in the row set, the column set or the box set.
Otherwise insert it into all three sets; return true once the scan finishes.
complexity: Time O(81) constant, space O(81)
pitfall: Trying to prove the board solvable, or indexing boxes as r // 3 + c // 3, which merges distinct boxes.
bruteForce: Separate passes that sort each row, column and box, still constant but far more traversal.

title: Combination Sum
insight: Unlimited reuse means recursing at the same index rather than the next one, and passing a start index (never restarting at 0) is what keeps reorderings out of the answer.
steps: Sort candidates so you can prune, since they are distinct positive integers.
Recurse with (start, remaining, path).
If remaining == 0 record a copy of path and return; if remaining < 0 return.
Loop i from start to n-1: push candidates[i], recurse with (i, remaining - candidates[i]), then pop.
Recursing at i and not i+1 is exactly what allows a number to repeat.
complexity: Time O(n^(target/min)) worst case, space O(target/min) depth
pitfall: Recursing from index 0 each time, which reports [2,3] and [3,2] as two different combinations.
bruteForce: Enumerate every multiset up to depth target/min and filter by sum, with no pruning.

title: Combination Sum II
insight: Each element is usable once, so recurse at i+1. Sorting first and skipping i > start with candidates[i] == candidates[i-1] removes duplicate combinations with no result set.
steps: Sort candidates so equal values sit next to each other.
Recurse with (start, remaining, path); record a copy and return when remaining hits 0.
Loop i from start: if i > start and candidates[i] == candidates[i-1], continue.
Break out of the loop when candidates[i] > remaining, since later values are no smaller.
Push candidates[i], recurse with (i+1, remaining - candidates[i]), then pop.
complexity: Time O(2^n) worst case, space O(n) depth
pitfall: Skipping on equality without the i > start guard, which also drops valid combinations that legitimately use a duplicated value twice.
bruteForce: Enumerate all 2^n subsets, sum each, and dedupe with a set of sorted tuples.

title: Trapping Rain Water
insight: Water over a bar is min(maxLeft, maxRight) minus its height. The side with the smaller running max is already decided, so that bar can be settled immediately.
steps: Set l = 0, r = n-1, leftMax = h[0], rightMax = h[n-1], total = 0.
While l < r, work on the side whose running max is smaller.
If leftMax < rightMax: advance l, set leftMax = max(leftMax, h[l]), add leftMax - h[l].
Otherwise: retreat r, set rightMax = max(rightMax, h[r]), add rightMax - h[r].
Return total; updating the max before adding keeps every contribution non-negative.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Using the global maximum for both sides, or adding before updating the running max, which yields negative contributions.
bruteForce: For each bar scan both ways for the tallest bar, O(n^2); prefix and suffix max arrays cost O(n) space.

title: Multiply Strings
insight: Digit i of one number times digit j of the other always lands in result positions i+j and i+j+1, so a flat array of m+n digits needs no row shifting at all.
steps: Return the string 0 immediately if either input is 0.
Allocate res of length m+n filled with zeros, indexed so the last slot is the ones digit.
For i from m-1 down to 0 and j from n-1 down to 0, let p = d1 * d2 + res[i+j+1].
Set res[i+j+1] = p % 10 and add p // 10 into res[i+j], which may itself exceed 9 temporarily.
Strip leading zeros from res and join the remaining digits into the answer string.
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(m+n)
pitfall: Forgetting to add the existing res[i+j+1] before taking the remainder, or returning a string with leading zeros.
bruteForce: Repeated addition num2 times, or converting to big integers, which the problem bans.

title: Jump Game II
insight: Index ranges behave like BFS levels: from the current reachable window you can reach the furthest index any member of it covers, and each window boundary costs one jump.
steps: Set jumps = 0, curEnd = 0, farthest = 0.
Scan i from 0 to n-2, since standing on the last index needs no further jump.
Update farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]).
When i reaches curEnd, increment jumps and set curEnd = farthest.
Return jumps; for n == 1 the loop never runs and 0 is returned.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Looping through n-1 inclusive, which counts one extra jump taken after you are already standing on the last index.
bruteForce: DP over each index trying every reachable step length, O(n^2).

title: Permutations
insight: Fix one slot at a time: swap each remaining candidate into the current slot, recurse on the suffix, then swap back. No used-marker array or prefix copying is required.
steps: Recurse with an index k meaning positions 0 through k-1 are already fixed.
When k == n, append a copy of nums to the results.
Loop i from k to n-1 and swap nums[k] with nums[i].
Recurse at k+1, then swap back so the array is restored for the next i.
Return the results; values are distinct, so every leaf is a new permutation.
complexity: Time O(n * n!), space O(n) depth plus output
pitfall: Appending the live array instead of a copy, so every stored result aliases one list and they all end up identical.
bruteForce: Generate all n^n assignments and keep the ones that use each value exactly once.

title: Rotate Image
insight: A 90 degree clockwise rotation is exactly a transpose followed by reversing each row, and both of those are in-place swaps needing no second matrix.
steps: Loop i from 0 to n-1 and j from i+1 to n-1, swapping m[i][j] with m[j][i].
Starting j at i+1 touches each pair once; starting at 0 would swap twice and undo itself.
Then reverse each row in place with two pointers meeting in the middle.
Mutate the matrix in place; nothing is returned by the signature.
For counter-clockwise instead, reverse the order of the rows first and then transpose.
complexity: Time O(n^2), space O(1)
pitfall: Transposing over the full index range, which swaps every pair twice and leaves the matrix exactly as it started.
bruteForce: Write into a fresh n by n matrix at position [j][n-1-i]; O(n^2) extra space, which the in-place rule forbids.

title: Group Anagrams
insight: Anagrams share a canonical form, so one pass that hashes each word to its sorted letters, or to a 26 slot count tuple, groups them without comparing any pair of words.
steps: Create a dict from key to a list of words.
For each word build the key: the sorted characters, or a tuple of 26 lowercase letter counts.
Append the original word to dict[key].
Return the dict values as a list of groups; both group order and inner order are free.
The empty string is a legal input word and forms its own group.
complexity: Time O(n*k log k) sorted keys, or O(n*k) with counts
pitfall: Keying on a sum or product of character codes, which collides across different letter multisets, or using a mutable list as the key.
bruteForce: Compare every pair of words for the anagram relation, O(n^2 * k).

title: Pow(x, n)
insight: x to the n halves at every step: square the base and halve the exponent, folding the base into the result whenever the current exponent bit is 1.
steps: Take m = n as a 64-bit value; if n is negative use m = -n and invert at the end.
Set res = 1.0 and base = x.
While m > 0: if m is odd set res *= base; then base *= base and m //= 2.
Return res for n >= 0, or 1 / res for n < 0.
n == 0 returns 1.0; constraints forbid x == 0 with n <= 0, so no 0^0 and no divide by zero.
complexity: Time O(log n), space O(1)
pitfall: Negating n when n is INT_MIN, which overflows 32-bit; widen to 64-bit first or peel off a single factor.
bruteForce: Multiply x by itself n times, O(n) with n as large as 2^31.

title: N-Queens
insight: Place exactly one queen per row and track attacked columns and both diagonals in sets keyed by col, row+col and row-col, making each legality test O(1).
steps: Recurse row by row carrying sets cols, diag (row+col) and anti (row-col), plus the chosen columns.
When row == n, render each chosen column as a string of dots with one Q and record the board.
For each column c in this row, skip it if c is in cols, row+c in diag, or row-c in anti.
Otherwise add all three keys, record c for this row, and recurse at row+1.
Remove the three keys and the recorded column before trying the next c.
complexity: Time O(n!) order, space O(n) plus output
pitfall: Using row+col for both diagonals, or rescanning the whole board for conflicts instead of keeping the three sets.
bruteForce: Try all n^n column assignments and validate each full board, hopeless beyond tiny n.

title: Maximum Subarray
insight: A running sum that has gone negative can never help any later subarray, so restart it at the current element. The answer is the best running sum ever seen.
steps: Initialise cur = best = nums[0], so an all-negative array still returns its largest element.
Scan i from 1 to n-1.
Set cur = max(nums[i], cur + nums[i]); that max is the restart decision.
Set best = max(best, cur) right after.
Return best; the array holds at least one element by the constraints.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Seeding best at 0, which returns 0 for an all-negative array instead of the least negative element.
bruteForce: Sum every subarray, O(n^2) with prefix sums or O(n^3) naively.

title: Spiral Matrix
insight: Hold four boundaries and peel one edge per step. After the top row and right column, the boundaries may have crossed, so re-check before the bottom row and left column.
steps: Set top = 0, bottom = m-1, left = 0, right = n-1 and an empty output list.
While top <= bottom and left <= right, walk left to right along row top, then top += 1.
Walk top to bottom down column right, then right -= 1.
If top <= bottom, walk right to left along row bottom, then bottom -= 1.
If left <= right, walk bottom to top up column left, then left += 1; return the output.
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(1) ignoring output
pitfall: Dropping the re-checks before the bottom row and left column, which double counts cells when a single row or column remains.
bruteForce: Simulate with a visited matrix, turning right at a wall or a visited cell, O(m*n) extra space.

title: Jump Game
insight: All you need is the furthest index reachable so far. If the scan ever stands on an index beyond that frontier, nothing earlier could jump there and the array is blocked.
steps: Set reach = 0.
Scan i from 0 to n-1.
Return false at once if i > reach, since no earlier index reaches this far.
Update reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]).
Return true after the loop, or break early once reach >= n-1.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Assuming any 0 in the array blocks you; a 0 only matters when it sits exactly on the reachability frontier.
bruteForce: DFS or DP from each index over all its jump lengths, O(n^2).

title: Merge Intervals
insight: Once sorted by start, a new interval can only overlap the block currently being accumulated, so one pass holding a single open interval is enough.
steps: Sort the intervals by start value.
Push the first interval onto an output list.
For each later interval, compare its start against the last output interval's end.
If start <= that end, merge by setting the end to max(existing end, this end).
Otherwise append it as a new block; return the output list.
complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n) output
pitfall: Overwriting the end instead of taking the max, which truncates a fully contained interval such as [1,10] followed by [2,3].
bruteForce: Repeatedly scan for any overlapping pair and merge it until a pass changes nothing, O(n^2) or worse.

title: Insert Interval
insight: The input is already sorted and disjoint, so one pass splits into intervals strictly before, the run that overlaps (collapsed into one), and intervals strictly after.
steps: Copy every interval whose end < newInterval start into the output unchanged.
While the current interval's start <= newInterval end, widen newInterval to min of starts and max of ends.
Append the widened newInterval once that overlap run ends.
Copy all remaining intervals across unchanged.
Return the output; an empty input yields a list holding only newInterval.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) output
pitfall: Treating touching intervals as disjoint; [1,3] and [3,5] overlap here, so the boundary comparisons must use <= not <.
bruteForce: Append the new interval, sort, then run the full merge-intervals routine, O(n log n).

title: Unique Paths
insight: Paths into a cell are paths from above plus paths from the left, so one row rolled down the grid suffices. It is also exactly the binomial C(m+n-2, m-1).
steps: Create row = [1] * n, meaning every cell of the top row has one path.
Repeat the following for each of the m-1 remaining rows.
Scan j from 1 to n-1 setting row[j] += row[j-1], which folds in the path from above.
Leave row[0] at 1, since the left column is reachable only by going straight down.
Return row[n-1]; the closed form C(m+n-2, m-1) gives the same number in O(min(m,n)).
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(n); O(min(m,n)) via the formula
pitfall: Starting the inner scan at j = 0 and wrapping to row[n-1], or computing the binomial with factorials that overflow before dividing.
bruteForce: Recursively branch right and down with no memo, exponential in m+n.

title: Plus One
insight: Only a trailing run of 9s can carry. The first digit below 9, scanning from the right, absorbs the increment and the loop can stop right there.
steps: Scan i from the last index down to 0.
If digits[i] < 9, increment it and return digits immediately.
Otherwise set digits[i] = 0 and keep moving left.
If the loop runs out, every digit was a 9.
Return a 1 followed by n zeros, that is an array one longer than the input.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1), or O(n) for the all-nines case
pitfall: Missing the all-nines case, which needs a longer array, or converting the digits to an integer and overflowing at 100 digits.
bruteForce: Join the digits into a number, add one, split back; overflows past 2^63 for long inputs.

title: Add Binary
insight: Walk both strings from the end with a carry. Each position emits (a + b + carry) mod 2 and carries the integer half, exactly like decimal addition but in base 2.
steps: Set i and j to the last indices of a and b, carry = 0, and an empty output buffer.
Loop while i >= 0 or j >= 0 or carry is nonzero.
Add the two current bits, treating an exhausted index as 0, plus carry, into s.
Append str(s % 2) to the buffer, set carry = s // 2, and decrement both indices.
Reverse the buffer and join it; a final carry is already included as the leading 1.
complexity: Time O(max(m,n)), space O(max(m,n))
pitfall: Ending the loop when the shorter string runs out, or dropping the final carry, so 1 plus 1 returns 0 instead of 10.
bruteForce: Parse both as integers, add, reformat to binary; overflows fixed width types at 10^4 bits.

title: Climbing Stairs
insight: You reach step n only from step n-1 or n-2, so the count follows the Fibonacci recurrence and only the last two values ever need to be kept.
steps: Return 1 when n == 1 so the seeding stays correct.
Set a = 1 (ways to reach step 1) and b = 2 (ways to reach step 2).
Loop n-2 times, each time setting a, b = b, a + b.
Return b, which now holds the number of ways to reach step n.
A top-down variant memoizes f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) with the same base cases.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Off by one seeding: taking f(1) as 2 or f(2) as 1 shifts the whole sequence by a step.
bruteForce: Recurse on f(n-1) + f(n-2) with no memo, O(2^n).

title: Edit Distance
insight: dp[i][j] is the distance between the first i and first j characters. Matching characters cost nothing; otherwise it is one plus the best of delete, insert and replace.
steps: Build a table of size (m+1) by (n+1) with dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j for the empty prefixes.
Loop i from 1 to m and j from 1 to n.
If word1[i-1] == word2[j-1], set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] with no cost added.
Else dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) for delete, insert, replace.
Return dp[m][n]; keeping only two rows cuts space to O(n).
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(m*n), or O(min(m,n)) rolling
pitfall: Leaving the first row and column as zeros, which makes deleting a whole prefix free and understates the distance.
bruteForce: Recurse on all three edits at every mismatch with no memo, about O(3^(m+n)).

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
pattern: First row and column as markers
insight: Store the flags inside the matrix itself: row 0 and column 0 record which lines must be cleared, with one extra boolean to remember column 0's own fate.
steps: Scan column 0 and remember in a boolean whether any cell in it is zero.
For every cell with c >= 1 that is zero, set m[r][0] = 0 and m[0][c] = 0 as markers.
Sweep the interior with r >= 1 and c >= 1, zeroing a cell when m[r][0] or m[0][c] is 0.
If m[0][0] == 0, zero the entire first row.
If the saved boolean is true, zero the entire first column; the mutation is the answer.
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(1)
pitfall: Zeroing cells during the first scan, which cascades and wipes the matrix, or mishandling the shared corner at m[0][0].
bruteForce: Collect zero row and column indices in two sets, then clear them, O(m+n) extra space.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
insight: Each row is sorted and every row's first value exceeds the previous row's last, so the matrix is one sorted sequence addressed by index // n and index % n.
steps: Set lo = 0 and hi = m*n - 1 over virtual flat indices.
While lo <= hi, take mid = (lo + hi) // 2 and read matrix[mid // n][mid % n].
Return true on an exact match.
Set lo = mid + 1 when that value is below target, hi = mid - 1 when above.
Return false after the loop; m and n are at least 1 by the constraints.
complexity: Time O(log(m*n)), space O(1)
pitfall: Decoding the flat index with m instead of n, which happens to work only for square matrices and fails otherwise.
bruteForce: Scan every cell, O(m*n); binary searching the row then within it is O(log m + log n), equally good.

title: Sort Colors
insight: Maintain three regions with two write pointers: before low is all 0s, after high is all 2s, and the scanner only advances when the value it just placed is known.
steps: Set low = 0, i = 0, high = n-1.
While i <= high, look at nums[i].
If it is 0, swap nums[i] with nums[low], then increment both low and i.
If it is 2, swap nums[i] with nums[high] and decrement high only, leaving i in place.
If it is 1, just increment i; the loop ends when i passes high and the array is sorted.
complexity: Time O(n) one pass, space O(1)
pitfall: Incrementing i after swapping a 2 to the back, which skips the value brought in from the right end without examining it.
bruteForce: Count the 0s, 1s and 2s, then overwrite the array; correct but a two pass solution.

title: Minimum Window Substring
insight: Track how many characters are still missing instead of comparing whole frequency maps. The window is valid the instant missing hits zero, and only then do you shrink from the left.
steps: Build need counts from t and set missing to t.length; set left to 0 and best to an empty range.
Move right over s: decrement need[c]; if need[c] was positive before that decrement, decrement missing.
While missing is 0, record the window if shorter than best, then advance left: increment need[s[left]].
If that incremented need[s[left]] becomes positive, increment missing, which ends the shrink loop.
Return the best recorded window, or the empty string if no valid window was ever seen.
complexity: Time O(m + n), space O(k) for k distinct chars in t
pitfall: Using a set rather than counts for t, so duplicated characters in t are satisfied by a single copy in the window.
bruteForce: Check all O(m^2) substrings of s, building counts for each: O(m^2 * (m + n)) time.

title: Subsets
insight: Each element is an independent binary choice, so the power set is exactly the 2^n bitmasks. Recursion on an index with one shared path list builds them without rebuilding at every level.
steps: Recurse on index i with a path list; at i == nums.length push a copy of path into the result.
Branch one: append nums[i] to path, recurse on i + 1, then pop it to restore the path.
Branch two: recurse on i + 1 without appending, covering the skip choice.
Alternatively loop mask from 0 to 2^n - 1 and collect nums[j] wherever bit j of mask is set.
The empty subset falls out naturally, so it needs no special case.
complexity: Time O(n * 2^n), space O(n) depth plus output
pitfall: Pushing the path list by reference instead of a copy, so every stored subset mutates as the recursion backtracks.
bruteForce: For each of the 2^n masks build the subset, then linear-scan the result list to check it is new: O(n * 4^n).

title: Word Search
insight: Mark the cell visited in place before recursing and restore it afterwards. That enforces no reuse on a single path and needs no separate visited matrix.
steps: For each cell, run dfs(r, c, 0) and return true on the first success.
In dfs, return false if out of bounds or board[r][c] != word[index].
Return true if index == word.length - 1, since the current char already matched.
Save the char, set board[r][c] to a sentinel such as '#', then recurse into all four neighbours.
Restore the saved char before returning, so other paths may legitimately use this cell.
complexity: Time O(m * n * 4^L), L = word length, space O(L)
pitfall: Forgetting to restore the cell after the recursive calls, which permanently blocks later paths that need it.
bruteForce: Enumerate every simple path of length L from each cell, then compare it to word: O(m * n * 4^L * L), no pruning.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
insight: A bar's maximal rectangle extends until a strictly shorter bar on each side. A stack of non-decreasing heights hands you the left boundary for free the moment you pop.
steps: Keep a stack of indices whose heights are non-decreasing; iterate i from 0 to n inclusive.
Treat the height at i == n as 0 so every remaining bar is forced off the stack.
While the stack is non-empty and the top's height exceeds heights[i], pop index j.
Height is heights[j]; width is i - 1 - newTop where newTop is the index now on top, or i if empty.
Update the running max area, then push i after the while loop to keep the stack non-decreasing.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the stack
pitfall: Getting the width wrong after a pop: it spans from the new stack top plus one through i - 1, not from j.
bruteForce: For every pair of bars take the minimum height times the span: O(n^2) time.

title: Subsets II
insight: Sort first, then at each recursion level use each distinct value at most once. Skipping nums[i] when it equals nums[i-1] and i is past the level's start prunes every duplicate branch.
steps: Sort nums so equal values sit adjacent.
Recurse with a start index; on entry push a copy of the current path into the result.
Loop i from start to n - 1; if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1], continue to skip the duplicate.
Append nums[i], recurse with start = i + 1, then pop to backtrack.
This emits the empty subset once and never emits the same multiset twice.
complexity: Time O(n * 2^n), space O(n) depth plus output
pitfall: Skipping on i > 0 instead of i > start, which wrongly drops valid subsets that contain a repeated value twice.
bruteForce: Generate all 2^n masks and dedupe with a hash set of sorted tuples: same time but O(n * 2^n) extra memory.

title: Decode Ways
pattern: Linear DP over two prior counts
insight: Ways to decode a prefix depend only on the last one or two digits: add dp[i-1] when s[i] is 1 to 9, and dp[i-2] when the pair s[i-1..i] reads 10 to 26.
steps: Return 0 if s[0] is '0'; otherwise set prev2 = 1 for the empty prefix and prev1 = 1.
For i from 1 to n - 1, start cur at 0.
If s[i] != '0', add prev1 to cur, taking s[i] as a one-digit code.
If the two-digit value of s[i-1..i] lies between 10 and 26, add prev2 to cur.
If cur is 0 the string is undecodable, so return 0; else set prev2 = prev1 and prev1 = cur.
Return prev1 after the loop.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Treating '0' as a standalone code or allowing '06' as a two-digit code; a leading zero makes the whole answer 0.
bruteForce: Recurse on every split into one or two digits with no memo: O(2^n) time.

title: Interleaving String
insight: Only how many characters you have consumed from s1 and s2 matters, not the order they were taken in, so dp[i][j] asks whether s1's first i and s2's first j chars build s3's first i+j.
steps: Return false unless s1.length + s2.length == s3.length.
Set dp[0][0] = true and iterate i from 0 to m, j from 0 to n, skipping i == j == 0.
dp[i][j] is true if i > 0 and dp[i-1][j] and s1[i-1] == s3[i+j-1].
Or if j > 0 and dp[i][j-1] and s2[j-1] == s3[i+j-1].
Return dp[m][n]; collapse to one rolling row of length n + 1 for O(n) space.
Empty s1 or s2 is handled by the base row and column, which just match s3 directly.
complexity: Time O(m * n), space O(n) with a rolling row
pitfall: Skipping the length check, which lets a mismatched s3 slip through, and mis-indexing s3 as i+j rather than i+j-1.
bruteForce: Try taking the next char from s1 or from s2 at every step: O(2^(m+n)) time.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
insight: Comparing a node only to its children is not enough: each node must sit inside a range inherited from all its ancestors, so pass (low, high) down and tighten one side at each turn.
steps: Call validate(root, low = null, high = null), where null means unbounded.
Return true on a null node.
Return false if low is set and node.val <= low, or high is set and node.val >= high.
Recurse left with (low, node.val) and right with (node.val, high); both must hold.
Alternatively walk inorder and verify each value is strictly greater than the previous one.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) for tree height h
pitfall: Using INT_MIN and INT_MAX as sentinel bounds when node values can equal exactly those, since comparisons are strict.
bruteForce: For each node scan its entire subtree to check every value: O(n^2) time.

title: Same Tree
insight: Recurse on both trees in lockstep. The pattern of nulls is itself part of the structure, so checking it at every position is what makes shape equality fall out.
steps: Return true if both p and q are null, which also covers two empty trees.
Return false if exactly one of p and q is null, catching every shape mismatch.
Return false if p.val != q.val.
Return the AND of recursing on (p.left, q.left) and (p.right, q.right).
No global state is needed, so the recursion is a pure structural comparison.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) for height h
pitfall: Comparing one serialized traversal: preorder alone does not determine shape unless null children are emitted as markers too.
bruteForce: Serialize both trees with null markers and compare strings: same O(n) time, but O(n) extra space for them.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
insight: Snapshot the queue length before draining a level: that count is exactly the nodes on that level, which carves one flat queue into per-level lists without storing any depths.
steps: Return an empty list if root is null.
Push root into a queue and loop while the queue is non-empty.
Snapshot size = queue.length, then pop exactly size nodes into a fresh level list.
For each popped node push its left child then its right child, skipping nulls.
Append the level list to the result; return the result once the queue drains.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(w) for the widest level w
pitfall: Reading queue.length inside the inner loop, which keeps growing as children are pushed and merges all levels into one.
bruteForce: Compute the height, then traverse the whole tree once per depth collecting that level: O(n * h).

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
insight: A node's depth is one plus the larger of its two subtree depths, so one bottom-up recursion settles it. Depth counts nodes, not edges, and the empty tree is 0.
steps: Return 0 when the node is null.
Recurse to get leftDepth and rightDepth.
Return 1 + max(leftDepth, rightDepth).
A single root with no children correctly returns 1.
Or run BFS and count how many level-drain rounds the queue survives.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(h), worst case O(n) when skewed
pitfall: Counting edges instead of nodes, so a one-node tree reports 0 when the expected answer is 1.
bruteForce: Build every root-to-leaf path as an explicit list and take the longest: O(n * h) time and space.

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
pattern: Divide and conquer with index map
insight: Preorder gives you the root first; its position in inorder splits the rest into the left and right subtrees. A value-to-index hash makes finding that split position O(1).
steps: Build a hash map from each inorder value to its index; values are unique so this is well defined.
Keep one preorder cursor starting at 0, shared across the whole recursion.
build(inLo, inHi): return null if inLo > inHi; take rootVal = preorder[cursor] and advance cursor.
Look up rootIdx = map[rootVal], then recurse build(inLo, rootIdx - 1) for the left child.
Then recurse build(rootIdx + 1, inHi) for the right child; this order is required by the shared cursor.
Return build(0, n - 1) as the tree root.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the map and recursion
pitfall: Building the right subtree before the left one: the shared preorder cursor then consumes values meant for the left side.
bruteForce: Linear-scan inorder for the root index at every level: O(n^2) on a skewed tree.

title: Balanced Binary Tree
insight: Return height and balance in a single value: have the recursion hand back -1 as a poison signal the moment any subtree is unbalanced, so each node is visited exactly once.
steps: Define height(node): return 0 if node is null.
Compute l = height(node.left) and return -1 at once if l is -1.
Compute r = height(node.right) and return -1 at once if r is -1.
Return -1 if abs(l - r) > 1, otherwise return 1 + max(l, r).
The tree is balanced if height(root) != -1; an empty tree is balanced.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) for tree height h
pitfall: Calling a separate height function inside the balance check at every node, which quietly degrades to O(n^2).
bruteForce: Recompute both subtree heights from scratch at each node: O(n^2) on a skewed tree.

title: Distinct Subsequences
insight: dp[i][j] counts the ways s's first i chars form t's first j chars. On a character match you may consume s[i-1] or skip it, so you add both cases; on a mismatch you can only skip.
steps: Allocate dp of size (m+1) x (n+1); set dp[i][0] = 1 since the empty t is matched exactly one way.
Leave dp[0][j] = 0 for j >= 1: a non-empty t cannot come from an empty s.
For i 1..m and j 1..n, start with dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j], the case where s[i-1] is skipped.
If s[i-1] == t[j-1], add dp[i-1][j-1], the case where s[i-1] is matched against t[j-1].
Return dp[m][n]; one rolling row iterated with j descending gives O(n) space.
complexity: Time O(m * n), space O(n) with a rolling row
pitfall: Iterating j ascending in the 1D rolling version, which clobbers dp[j-1] before you read the previous row's value from it.
bruteForce: Enumerate all 2^m subsequences of s and compare each to t: O(2^m * n) time.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
insight: If you sell on day i, your best buy is the cheapest price seen strictly before i. Carrying that minimum forward collapses the whole problem into one pass.
steps: Set minPrice = prices[0] and best = 0.
For i from 1 to n - 1, compute profit = prices[i] - minPrice.
Update best if profit exceeds the current best.
Then update minPrice = min(minPrice, prices[i]), after taking the profit.
Return best, which stays 0 when prices only ever fall.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Updating minPrice before taking the profit, which permits buying and selling on the same day, or returning a negative profit.
bruteForce: Check every buy-sell pair with i < j: O(n^2) time.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
insight: Keep two quantities apart: the best path that bends at a node (left arm plus node plus right arm, folded into a global max) and the best straight arm handed upward, which may use only one child.
steps: Keep a global best initialised to negative infinity, not to 0.
gain(node): return 0 if node is null, so an absent branch contributes nothing.
Compute left = max(0, gain(node.left)) and right = max(0, gain(node.right)), clipping negatives.
Update best with node.val + left + right, the path that bends at this node.
Return node.val + max(left, right) upward, since only one arm can continue.
Return best after the walk; an all-negative tree yields its largest single node.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) for tree height h
pitfall: Returning node.val + left + right upward, which stitches together an invalid branching path instead of a simple one.
bruteForce: Sum the path between every pair of nodes, single nodes included: about O(n^2 * h) time for height h.

title: Valid Palindrome
insight: You never need a cleaned copy of the string: walk one pointer in from each end, skip anything non-alphanumeric, and compare lowercased characters in place.
steps: Set i = 0 and j = s.length - 1.
While i < j, advance i while i < j and s[i] is not alphanumeric.
Decrement j while i < j and s[j] is not alphanumeric.
Compare lowercase s[i] with lowercase s[j] and return false on any mismatch.
Otherwise do i++ and j-- and continue; return true if the loop completes.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Forgetting digits count as alphanumeric, or dropping the i < j guard inside the skip loops and walking past the other pointer.
bruteForce: Filter and lowercase into a new string, then compare it with its reverse: same O(n) time but O(n) space.

title: Word Ladder
insight: This is unweighted shortest path, so BFS depth is the answer. Generate neighbours by substituting all 26 letters at each position rather than comparing every pair of words.
steps: Put wordList into a hash set and return 0 at once if endWord is not in that set.
Seed a queue with beginWord at distance 1 and erase beginWord from the set if present.
Pop a word; if it equals endWord return its distance.
For each position try all 26 letters: if the candidate is in the set, erase it and push it at distance + 1.
Erasing on enqueue rather than on dequeue stops the same word entering the queue twice.
Return 0 if the queue drains without ever reaching endWord.
complexity: Time O(N * L * 26), N words of length L; space O(N * L)
pitfall: Not checking endWord is in wordList, which must return 0, or marking visited at dequeue time so duplicates pile up in the queue.
bruteForce: Build the graph by comparing all word pairs, then BFS: O(N^2 * L) just to construct it.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
pattern: Hash set, expand from run starts
insight: Only begin counting at a value whose predecessor is absent. Every element is then touched by exactly one upward walk, which is what keeps the total linear despite the inner loop.
steps: Return 0 if nums is empty, which the constraints allow.
Put all nums into a hash set, which also collapses duplicates.
For each value v in the set, skip it if v - 1 is also in the set: v is not a run start.
Otherwise walk v + 1, v + 2 and onward while present, counting the run length.
Track the maximum run length seen and return it.
complexity: Time O(n) expected, space O(n)
pitfall: Dropping the v - 1 guard, which re-walks every run from each of its members and degrades to O(n^2) on one long run.
bruteForce: Sort and scan adjacent values skipping duplicates: O(n log n), which breaks the stated O(n) requirement.

title: Surrounded Regions
insight: Invert the question: a region survives only if it touches the edge. Flood fill every border 'O' to a temporary mark, and whatever is still 'O' afterwards must be enclosed.
steps: For every cell on the four borders that holds 'O', launch a DFS or BFS flood fill.
The fill rewrites connected 'O' cells to a sentinel such as 'T', stopping at 'X' and at the bounds.
After all border fills finish, sweep the whole board once.
Turn every remaining 'O' into 'X', since it cannot reach the edge.
Turn every 'T' back into 'O', restoring the survivors in place.
Prefer BFS on a 200 by 200 board so a snaking region cannot blow the recursion stack.
complexity: Time O(m * n), space O(m * n) for the frontier
pitfall: Flood filling interior regions and testing afterwards whether they touched an edge, which is far easier to get wrong.
bruteForce: For each interior 'O' explore its whole region hunting for a border cell, with no memo: O((m * n)^2) time.

title: Palindrome Partitioning
insight: Fix the start of the next piece and try every end: if that prefix is a palindrome, recurse on the remainder. Precomputing an isPal table removes the repeated linear checks.
steps: Precompute isPal[i][j] by increasing substring length, or check palindromes inline with two pointers.
Recurse with a start index; when start == s.length push a copy of the path into the result.
Loop end from start to n - 1 and skip unless s[start..end] is a palindrome.
Push that substring, recurse with start = end + 1, then pop to backtrack.
Single characters are palindromes, so a full split always exists and the result is never empty.
complexity: Time O(n * 2^n), space O(n^2) table plus O(n) depth
pitfall: Re-slicing and re-testing the same substrings at every level, or pushing the path by reference so backtracking corrupts stored answers.
bruteForce: Generate all 2^(n-1) cut sets and validate each piece: same O(n * 2^n) bound, but no cutoff on a bad prefix.

title: Clone Graph
insight: The map from original node to clone serves as both memo and visited set. Create the clone and record it before recursing, or a cycle sends you into infinite recursion.
steps: Return null if the given node is null, since the graph may be empty.
Keep a hash map keyed by original node, valued by its clone.
dfs(node): if node is already a key in the map, return the stored clone.
Create a clone with the same val, store it in the map immediately, then recurse into neighbours.
Push dfs(neighbour) into the clone's neighbour list for each neighbour.
Return the clone of the entry node.
complexity: Time O(V + E), space O(V) for the map and recursion
pitfall: Recursing into neighbours before inserting the new clone into the map, which loops forever on any cycle in the graph.
bruteForce: Linear-scan a list of already-made clones to find each neighbour's copy instead of hashing: O(V * (V + E)).

title: Gas Station
insight: A solution exists exactly when total gas is at least total cost. Any prefix where the running tank dips negative cannot contain the start, so reset the candidate to the next station.
steps: Set total = 0, tank = 0, start = 0.
For i from 0 to n - 1, add gas[i] - cost[i] to both total and tank.
If tank goes negative, set start = i + 1 and reset tank to 0.
After the loop, return -1 if total is negative: no start can work.
Otherwise return start, which is the unique valid starting index.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Returning start without the total check: the reset logic alone cannot distinguish an infeasible circuit from a feasible one.
bruteForce: Simulate the full circuit from each of the n possible starts: O(n^2) time.

title: Single Number
insight: XOR is its own inverse and is order independent, so every value appearing twice cancels to 0 and folding the whole array leaves exactly the lone element.
steps: Set acc = 0.
For each value v in nums, set acc = acc XOR v.
Pairs vanish because v XOR v is 0, and 0 XOR x is x.
Return acc once the pass completes.
Negative values are fine: two's complement bits cancel in exactly the same way.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Reaching for a hash set or a sort, which breaks the stated constant extra space requirement even though it gets the right answer.
bruteForce: Count occurrences in a hash map and take the key with count 1: O(n) space, which the constant-space rule forbids.

title: Copy List with Random Pointer
insight: Weave each clone immediately after its original, so original.next is its own copy. Then clone.random is simply original.random.next, with no map needed at all.
steps: Return null for an empty list.
Pass one: for each original node, splice in a new node with the same val directly after it.
Pass two: for each original o, set o.next.random to o.random.next, or null when o.random is null.
Pass three: unweave, restoring each original's next while linking the clones to each other.
Return the clone head, captured as the original head's next before unweaving begins.
The simpler route is a hash map from original to clone plus a second rewiring pass, at O(n) space.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) extra with the weave method
pitfall: Dereferencing a null random pointer in the second pass, or leaving the original list's next pointers mangled at the end.
bruteForce: For each random pointer walk the list to find its index, then walk the clone to that index: O(n^2).

title: Word Break
insight: dp[i] means s's first i chars are segmentable. It holds if some j < i has dp[j] true and s[j..i-1] in the dictionary, so each position only consults booleans before it.
steps: Put wordDict into a hash set and record L, the longest word length.
Allocate dp of size n + 1 with dp[0] = true for the empty prefix.
For i from 1 to n, loop j from max(0, i - L) up to i - 1.
If dp[j] is true and s.slice(j, i) is in the set, set dp[i] = true and break the inner loop.
Return dp[n]; capping the inner loop at L avoids pointless long slices.
complexity: Time O(n * L^2), L the longest word; space O(n)
pitfall: Greedily taking the longest matching word at each position, which fails on inputs like 'aaaaab' where you must backtrack.
bruteForce: Recurse on every split point with no memoisation: O(2^n) time.

title: Linked List Cycle
insight: Advance one pointer by one node and another by two. Inside a cycle the gap closes by one each step so they must meet; on a straight list the fast one runs off the end.
steps: Set slow = head and fast = head.
Loop while fast and fast.next are both non-null.
Advance slow by one node and fast by two nodes.
Return true if slow and fast now reference the same node.
Return false when the loop exits, which also covers empty and single-node lists.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Dereferencing fast.next.next without first guarding both fast and fast.next, which crashes on an even-length acyclic list.
bruteForce: Store visited nodes in a hash set and stop on a repeat: same O(n) time but O(n) space, which the follow-up bars.

title: Reorder List
insight: The target order is the first half zipped with the reversed second half, so split at the midpoint, reverse the tail in place, then alternate nodes from the two lists.
steps: Find the middle with slow and fast pointers; slow ends on the last node of the first half.
Sever the halves: set second = slow.next, then slow.next = null.
Reverse the second list in place with the prev, cur, next three-pointer loop.
Merge by alternately taking one node from the first list and one from the reversed second.
The first half is equal or one longer, so it supplies the final node and the merge terminates cleanly.
Lists of one or two nodes are already in the target order and fall straight out of this.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Not severing the first half before reversing, which leaves the merged result cyclic and makes traversal loop forever.
bruteForce: Push all nodes into an array and rewire pointers by index from both ends: same O(n) time but O(n) space.

title: LRU Cache
pattern: Hash map plus doubly linked list
insight: A hash map gives O(1) lookup but no ordering; a doubly linked list gives O(1) move and evict but no lookup. Map each key to its list node and you get both at once.
steps: Keep a doubly linked list with dummy head and tail sentinels; the head side is most recently used.
Keep a map from key to its list node, where the node stores both key and value.
get(key): on a miss return -1; on a hit unlink the node, reinsert it after head, return its value.
put on an existing key: overwrite the value and move that node to just after head.
put on a new key: insert a node after head and add the map entry.
If the size now exceeds capacity, unlink the node before tail and delete its key from the map.
complexity: Time O(1) per get and put, space O(capacity)
pitfall: Evicting the list node without deleting its map entry, leaving a stale key, or forgetting that an update also counts as a use.
bruteForce: Keep a timestamp per key and scan for the oldest on eviction: O(n) per put, which the stated O(1) rule forbids.

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
insight: RPN needs no precedence or parenthesis handling: push numbers, and on an operator pop exactly two operands. Order matters, so the second pop is the left-hand side.
steps: Scan tokens left to right with a stack of integers.
If the token is not one of + - * /, parse it as an integer and push it.
Otherwise pop b, then pop a, so the expression evaluates as a op b.
Push a + b, a - b, a * b, or a / b with division truncated toward zero.
Return the single value remaining on the stack.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the stack
pitfall: Swapping operand order for - and /, or letting the language floor the division so -7 / 2 yields -4 rather than the required -3.
bruteForce: Repeatedly rescan for the leftmost operator with two numeric operands and collapse it: O(n^2) time.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
insight: A negative factor swaps the roles of the best and worst products, so you must carry the running minimum too. Allowing the current element alone handles zeros by restarting.
steps: Set curMax, curMin and best all to nums[0].
For i from 1 to n - 1, let v = nums[i] and save oldMax = curMax before updating anything.
Set curMax = max(v, oldMax * v, curMin * v).
Set curMin = min(v, oldMax * v, curMin * v), using the saved oldMax not the new curMax.
Update best = max(best, curMax).
Return best; including v alone is what lets a zero cut the subarray and restart.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Overwriting curMax before computing curMin, so curMin is derived from the already-updated value and silently goes wrong.
bruteForce: Multiply out every subarray and keep the largest: O(n^2) time.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
insight: Compare the midpoint against the right end, not the left. If nums[mid] > nums[hi] the minimum lies strictly right of mid; otherwise mid is itself still a candidate.
steps: Set lo = 0 and hi = n - 1.
While lo < hi, compute mid = lo + floor((hi - lo) / 2).
If nums[mid] > nums[hi], set lo = mid + 1 since the dip must be to the right.
Otherwise set hi = mid, keeping mid as a possible answer rather than discarding it.
Return nums[lo] when lo == hi; a fully rotated array correctly yields nums[0].
complexity: Time O(log n), space O(1)
pitfall: Comparing nums[mid] to nums[lo], which cannot separate the halves without extra cases; note elements are unique here, unlike problem 154.
bruteForce: Scan the array for the smallest value: O(n) time, which misses the required O(log n).

title: Min Stack
insight: Store alongside each value the minimum of the stack at the moment it was pushed. Popping then restores the previous minimum for free, with no rescanning.
steps: Keep one stack of pairs (value, minSoFar), or two stacks pushed and popped in lockstep.
push(v): newMin is v when the stack is empty, else min(v, top's minSoFar).
Push the pair (v, newMin).
pop(): discard the top pair, which drops its minSoFar along with it.
top() returns the top pair's value and getMin() returns the top pair's minSoFar.
Values may be exactly INT_MIN, so branch on emptiness instead of seeding a sentinel minimum.
complexity: Time O(1) per operation, space O(n)
pitfall: Keeping a single min variable: once you pop that minimum there is no way to recover the previous one without an O(n) scan.
bruteForce: Scan the whole stack on each getMin: O(n) per query, which the stated O(1)-per-operation rule forbids.

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
insight: Because the array is sorted, the outer pair's sum tells you which side to move: too large means the right index must shrink, too small means the left must grow.
steps: Set i = 0 and j = numbers.length - 1.
While i < j, compute sum = numbers[i] + numbers[j].
If sum == target, return [i + 1, j + 1] because this problem is 1-indexed.
If sum > target, decrement j: the current j cannot pair with anything smaller than numbers[i].
Otherwise increment i; keeping i < j guarantees no element is used twice.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Returning 0-based indices: this variant wants 1-based ones, unlike the original Two Sum.
bruteForce: Try every pair for O(n^2) time, or use hash lookups, which the constant-extra-space rule forbids.

title: Majority Element
insight: Pair off each occurrence of the majority element against a different value. Since it holds strictly more than half the slots, it outlives every cancellation and ends as the candidate.
steps: Set candidate to nums[0] and count to 0.
For each value v in nums: if count is 0, set candidate = v.
Increment count when v == candidate, otherwise decrement it.
Return candidate after the single pass.
No verification pass is needed here because the problem guarantees a majority exists.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Assuming the candidate is always the true mode: without the strict majority guarantee you must recount it in a second pass.
bruteForce: Count every value in a hash map, or sort and take nums[n / 2]: O(n) space or O(n log n) time.

title: Reverse Bits
insight: Shift the result left and push in the input's lowest bit, repeated exactly 32 times. The fixed width is the whole point, so leading zeros must be shifted through as well.
steps: Set result to 0.
Repeat exactly 32 times, never stopping early: shift result left by one.
OR in n AND 1, the current lowest bit of n.
Then shift n right by one, using an unsigned shift in languages with signed integers.
Return result, in JavaScript as result >>> 0 so it reads as an unsigned value.
The O(1) trick is swapping 16-bit halves, then 8, 4, 2 and 1 with fixed masks.
complexity: Time O(1), 32 fixed iterations; space O(1)
pitfall: Stopping once n reaches 0, which drops the remaining leading zeros and leaves every bit at the wrong position in the 32-bit result.
bruteForce: Format n as a 32-char binary string, reverse it, parse it back: also O(1), but allocates a string per call.

title: Number of 1 Bits
insight: n AND (n - 1) clears exactly the lowest set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit instead of once per bit position.
steps: Set count to 0.
While n is non-zero, set n = n AND (n - 1).
Increment count on each such clearing, since each one removed exactly one set bit.
Return count once n reaches 0.
The simpler variant tests n AND 1 and shifts right, running a fixed 32 times.
complexity: Time O(set bits), at most 32; space O(1)
pitfall: Writing n AND (n - 1) without assigning the result back to n, which leaves the loop condition unchanged and spins forever.
bruteForce: Test all 32 bit positions one at a time: O(32) regardless of how few bits are actually set.

title: House Robber
pattern: Linear DP with two rolling vars
insight: At each house you either skip it and keep the previous best, or take it plus the best from two houses back. Only those two numbers matter, so no array is required.
steps: Set prev2 = 0, the best through house i - 2, and prev1 = 0, the best through i - 1.
For each value v in nums, compute cur = max(prev1, prev2 + v).
Shift the window: prev2 = prev1, then prev1 = cur.
Return prev1 after the loop.
Starting both at 0 handles a single house correctly, returning nums[0].
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Assuming the answer strictly alternates houses: the optimum can skip two in a row, as in [2, 1, 1, 2] where you take 2 and 2.
bruteForce: Try every subset of non-adjacent houses: O(2^n) time.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
pattern: BFS taking each level's last node
insight: The visible node at each depth is the rightmost node on that level, so a level-by-level BFS simply records the last node it drained in each round.
steps: Return an empty list if root is null.
Push root into a queue and loop while the queue is non-empty.
Snapshot size, then pop exactly size nodes, pushing each node's non-null children.
Append the value of the last node popped in that round to the result.
Or DFS visiting the right child first and record a value whenever depth equals the result length.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(w) for the widest level w
pitfall: Following only right children: when the rightmost branch ends early, a deeper node in a left subtree becomes the visible one.
bruteForce: For each depth traverse the whole tree collecting that level, then take its last node: O(n * h).

title: Number of Islands
pattern: Flood fill per unvisited land cell
insight: Count how many times you have to start a fresh flood fill. Sinking each visited cell to '0' as you go means every cell is entered once across the entire run.
steps: Set count to 0 and scan every cell of the grid in row-major order.
Skip any cell that is not '1'.
On a '1', increment count and launch a flood fill from that cell.
The fill sets the cell to '0' and then visits its four in-bounds neighbours that are '1'.
Return count; sinking cells during the fill is exactly what prevents double counting.
Use BFS rather than DFS if a 300 by 300 snaking island might overflow the recursion stack.
complexity: Time O(m * n), space O(m * n) for the frontier
pitfall: Marking cells visited after dequeuing rather than when enqueuing, which pushes the same cell repeatedly and can time out.
bruteForce: Run a fresh BFS from each land cell and group cells by which set they reach: about O((m * n)^2) time.

title: Happy Number
insight: The digit-square map always eventually repeats, so this is cycle detection on a functional graph. Floyd's slow and fast pointers settle it in constant space.
steps: Define next(x) as the sum of the squares of x's decimal digits.
Set slow = n and fast = next(n).
Loop while fast != 1 and slow != fast.
Advance slow = next(slow) and fast = next(next(fast)) each iteration.
Return true if fast == 1, else false because slow met fast inside a cycle.
A hash set of values already seen works equally well, at O(log n) space.
complexity: Time O(log n) per step with bounded steps, space O(1)
pitfall: Iterating with no cycle guard at all, which spins forever on an unhappy number such as 2.
bruteForce: Iterate and store every value seen in a hash set until a repeat or 1: same time, O(log n) extra space.

title: Reverse Linked List
insight: Walk the list once, flipping each next pointer to the node you just came from. You must save the next node before overwriting the pointer or you lose the untraversed rest.
steps: Set prev = null and cur = head.
While cur is non-null, save nxt = cur.next first.
Set cur.next = prev, flipping this link backwards.
Advance prev = cur and then cur = nxt.
Return prev, which is the old tail and the new head.
An empty list returns null, since prev never moves off null.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Overwriting cur.next before saving it, which detaches and permanently loses the remainder of the list.
bruteForce: Collect values into an array and write them back in reverse order: same O(n) time but O(n) space.

title: Course Schedule
insight: A valid schedule exists exactly when the prerequisite digraph is acyclic, so you never need the order itself, only proof that every node can be peeled off by indegree.
steps: Build an adjacency list prereq to course plus an indegree array of size numCourses.
Push every course with indegree 0 into a queue; those need no prerequisites.
Pop a course, increment a counter, and decrement the indegree of each neighbour.
Push any neighbour whose indegree hits 0; repeat until the queue empties.
Return true only if the counter equals numCourses, else a cycle blocked some nodes.
complexity: Time O(V + E), space O(V + E)
pitfall: Building edges in the wrong direction, or returning true when the queue empties without having popped every course.
bruteForce: Check every permutation of courses against the prerequisite list, O(n! n).

title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
insight: Put characters on edges, not in nodes, and keep one boolean per node for 'a word ends here' so search and startsWith differ only in that final flag check.
steps: Define a node with 26 child slots (or a hash map) and an isWord flag; keep one root node.
insert: walk the word, creating any missing child, then set isWord on the last node.
Write a helper that walks a string and returns the final node, or null if a child is missing.
search: the helper returns a node and that node has isWord true.
startsWith: the helper returns any non-null node.
complexity: Time O(L) per op for word length L, space O(total chars)
pitfall: Returning true from search for a prefix that exists only inside a longer word, because isWord was never checked.
bruteForce: Keep a hash set of words and scan every word for prefix queries, O(n L) per startsWith.

title: Course Schedule II
insight: Kahn's queue produces a valid order as a byproduct. If fewer than numCourses nodes ever leave the queue the graph has a cycle and you must return an empty array.
steps: Build prereq to course adjacency and indegree counts over numCourses nodes.
Seed a queue with every indegree 0 course; the seeding order is free.
Pop a course, append it to the output, and decrement each neighbour's indegree.
Enqueue neighbours reaching indegree 0, so queued nodes always have all prereqs placed.
Return the output if its length is numCourses, otherwise return an empty array.
complexity: Time O(V + E), space O(V + E)
pitfall: Returning the partial order on a cyclic graph instead of an empty array, or dropping courses that have no edges at all.
bruteForce: Repeatedly rescan all courses for one whose prereqs are taken, O(V^2 + VE).

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
pattern: Trie with DFS over the dot wildcard
insight: Only a dot forces branching, so search is an ordinary trie walk that fans out into all 26 children exactly at dot positions and nowhere else.
steps: Build a trie node with 26 children plus an isWord flag; addWord inserts as usual.
Write dfs(node, index): if index equals the word length, return node.isWord.
If word[index] is a letter, recurse into that one child, returning false when it is null.
If it is a dot, recurse into every non-null child and return true on the first success.
search calls dfs(root, 0); words are at most 25 chars with at most 2 dots, so fanout is bounded.
complexity: Time O(26^d * L) for d dots, space O(L) recursion
pitfall: Treating a dot as matching zero or more characters; it matches exactly one, so the length must still line up exactly.
bruteForce: Store words in a list and regex match each one on every search, O(n L) per query.

title: Word Search II
pattern: Trie plus DFS backtracking on grid
insight: Searching each word separately rescans the board. Push all words into one trie and walk the board once, pruning a branch the moment the current prefix leaves the trie.
steps: Insert every word into a trie, storing the full word at its terminal node.
DFS from each cell carrying the matching trie node; mark the cell visited with a sentinel char.
On a node holding a word, add it to the result and clear the stored word to avoid duplicates.
Recurse into the four neighbours only when the trie child for that letter exists.
Restore the original cell letter when backtracking so other paths can reuse it.
Optionally prune dead leaf trie nodes after a hit to shrink later searches.
complexity: Time O(m n 4^L), space O(sum word lengths)
pitfall: Forgetting to unmark the visited cell on the way out, or emitting the same word twice when two paths reach it.
bruteForce: Run a separate grid DFS per word from every cell, O(W m n 4^L).

title: House Robber II
insight: The circle only forbids taking house 0 and house n-1 together, so the answer is the best linear solution excluding the last house versus excluding the first.
steps: Handle n equals 1 by returning nums[0]; the two-slice trick breaks on a single house.
Write a helper solving the linear case with two rolling scalars prev and curr.
In the helper set newCurr to max(curr, prev + nums[i]), then shift prev to the old curr.
Call the helper on nums[0..n-2] and again on nums[1..n-1].
Return the larger of the two helper results.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Skipping the n equals 1 base case, where both slices are empty and the helper wrongly returns 0.
bruteForce: Enumerate every subset of non-adjacent houses around the circle, O(2^n).

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
insight: You do not need the array sorted, only the value that lands at index n-k, so recurse into just the side of the pivot that contains that index.
steps: Convert k into the target index n-k under ascending order.
Pick a random pivot inside the current range and partition the values around it.
If the pivot settles on the target index, return that value.
Otherwise recurse into only the side containing the target, shrinking the range each round.
Switch to a size-k min-heap, O(n log k), when worst-case guarantees matter.
complexity: Time O(n) average, O(n^2) worst, space O(1)
pitfall: A fixed first-element pivot degrades to O(n^2) on sorted or all-equal input; randomise the pivot or partition three ways.
bruteForce: Sort the array and index n-k, O(n log n).

title: Contains Duplicate
insight: You can answer the instant one value repeats, so stream the array into a set and bail out on the first element already present.
steps: Create an empty hash set.
Iterate the array once, testing membership before inserting.
Return true immediately if the value is already in the set.
Insert the value and continue to the next index.
Return false after the loop; empty and single-element arrays fall through here.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n)
pitfall: Comparing set size to array length only at the very end, which is correct but loses the early exit on huge inputs.
bruteForce: Compare every pair of indices, O(n^2) time and O(1) space.

title: Basic Calculator
pattern: Stack of running result and sign
insight: With only plus, minus and parentheses there is no precedence to handle: keep a running total and a current sign, and push that pair when a bracket opens.
steps: Track result 0, sign +1, and a scanning index, skipping spaces as you go.
On a digit, consume the whole multi-digit number and add sign times its value to result.
On a plus or minus, set sign to +1 or -1 respectively.
On an open bracket, push result and sign, then reset result to 0 and sign to +1.
On a close bracket, pop sign and prev, setting result to prev + poppedSign * result.
Return result; a leading minus or a minus right after a bracket works since sign resets to +1.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for nesting depth
pitfall: Reading one digit at a time so multi-digit numbers break, or mishandling unary minus at the start or just after an open bracket.
bruteForce: Recursively locate matching brackets and evaluate inner substrings, O(n^2).

title: Invert Binary Tree
insight: Inverting is just swapping every node's two children. The recursion ignores values entirely and the order of swapping versus recursing does not matter.
steps: Return null immediately when the node is null, which covers the empty tree.
Recursively invert the left subtree and the right subtree.
Swap the node's left and right pointers using a temp variable.
Return the node so the caller can reattach it.
For an iterative version, push the root on a stack and swap children as each node pops.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) recursion for height h
pitfall: Assigning one child before saving the other, which overwrites and loses an entire subtree.
bruteForce: Build a brand new mirrored tree by copying every node, O(n) time and O(n) extra space.
