title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
insight: Inorder traversal of a BST emits values in sorted order, so stop at the kth visit rather than materialising the whole traversal.
steps: Keep an explicit stack and a pointer starting at the root.
Push nodes while walking left as far as the pointer can go.
Pop a node, decrement k, and return its value the moment k reaches 0.
Otherwise move the pointer to the popped node's right child and repeat.
If kth queries are frequent, store subtree sizes per node to answer in O(h).
complexity: Time O(h + k), space O(h) for height h
pitfall: Collecting the full traversal into a list, which costs O(n) even when k is 1, plus off-by-one because k is 1-indexed.
bruteForce: Gather all values inorder into a list and return index k-1, O(n) time and space.

title: Implement Queue using Stacks
insight: Reversing once is enough: push onto an input stack, pop from an output stack, and only refill output when it is completely empty.
steps: Keep stacks named in and out; push always goes onto in.
Define a transfer step that moves all of in onto out, but only when out is empty.
pop: run the transfer step, then pop from out.
peek: run the transfer step, then peek the top of out.
empty: true only when both stacks are empty.
complexity: Time O(1) amortized per op, space O(n)
pitfall: Transferring while out is still non-empty, which interleaves old and new elements and silently breaks FIFO order.
bruteForce: Shuttle every element between the two stacks on each pop, O(n) per operation.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
insight: The split point is the LCA: walk down from the root and the first node whose value sits between p and q, inclusive, is the answer.
steps: Start at the root with a plain while loop; no recursion or extra space is needed.
If both p.val and q.val are less than node.val, move to the left child.
If both are greater than node.val, move to the right child.
Otherwise the values straddle node.val or one equals it, so return node.
Both nodes are guaranteed to exist, so the loop always terminates on a real node.
complexity: Time O(h), space O(1) for height h
pitfall: Using strict inequalities that ignore the case where p or q is itself the ancestor, so the walk sails past the answer.
bruteForce: Build both root-to-node paths and compare them position by position, O(n) time and space.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
insight: Have each call report whether p or q lives in its subtree. The first node receiving a non-null report from both sides, or that is itself p or q, is the LCA.
steps: Return null when node is null; return node when it is p or q.
Recurse on the left and right children, capturing both returned values.
If both returns are non-null, this node is the split point, so return it.
Otherwise return whichever return is non-null, propagating the find upward.
Both p and q are guaranteed present, so one non-null return means the LCA is higher up.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) recursion for height h
pitfall: Returning at the first match is safe only because both nodes are guaranteed to exist; without that guarantee you would have to confirm both were actually found.
bruteForce: Record parent pointers by BFS, push p's ancestors into a set, then climb from q, O(n) space.

title: Product of Array Except Self
insight: Each answer is everything left of i times everything right of i, so two sweeps replace division and handle zeros without any special casing.
steps: Allocate the output array and set out[0] to 1.
Left sweep: out[i] = out[i-1] * nums[i-1], so out now holds strict prefix products.
Keep a running suffix scalar initialised to 1.
Right sweep from n-1 down: multiply out[i] by suffix, then multiply suffix by nums[i].
Return out; only the running scalar is extra space beyond the result array.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) extra beyond the output
pitfall: Reaching for total product divided by nums[i], which is disallowed and breaks on any zero in the array.
bruteForce: For each i multiply the other n-1 values, O(n^2), which the required O(n) bound rules out.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
insight: A value smaller than something arriving later can never be a maximum again, so hold indices in decreasing value order and the deque front is always the window max.
steps: Use a deque of indices whose values decrease from front to back.
For each i, pop from the back while nums[back] is less than or equal to nums[i], then push i.
Pop from the front while the front index is less than or equal to i - k, dropping expired entries.
Once i is at least k-1, append nums[front] to the answer array.
Store indices rather than values so expiry can be tested by position.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(k)
pitfall: Storing values instead of indices, so you cannot evict the element that just slid out, or emitting output before the first full window.
bruteForce: Scan each of the n-k+1 windows for its maximum, O(n k).

title: Valid Anagram
insight: Anagrams must have identical character multisets, so one counter array incremented by s and decremented by t has to end up all zeros.
steps: Return false immediately when the two lengths differ.
Allocate 26 counters for lowercase input, or a hash map for the unicode follow-up.
Increment the counter for every character of s.
Decrement for every character of t, returning false as soon as a counter goes negative.
Return true; equal lengths plus no negative means every counter is exactly zero.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) for a fixed alphabet
pitfall: Hardcoding 26 lowercase slots when the follow-up asks about unicode, where out-of-range characters are silently dropped.
bruteForce: Sort both strings and compare them, O(n log n).

title: Meeting Rooms
pattern: Sort by start, check adjacent pairs
insight: After sorting by start time any conflict must involve two neighbours, so a single linear scan comparing each start to the previous end settles the whole question.
steps: Return true for zero or one interval; nothing can conflict.
Sort the intervals by start time ascending.
Scan from index 1 comparing intervals[i][0] against intervals[i-1][1].
Return false the moment a start is strictly less than the previous end.
Return true after the scan; touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3] do not conflict.
complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(1) beyond the sort
pitfall: Using less than or equal when comparing a start to the previous end, which wrongly rejects back-to-back meetings sharing an endpoint.
bruteForce: Test every pair of intervals for overlap, O(n^2).

title: Meeting Rooms II
insight: Process meetings by start time and always reuse the room freeing earliest. The heap size is the rooms currently in use, so its peak over the sweep is the answer.
steps: Return 0 for an empty list, then sort the intervals by start time.
Keep a min-heap holding the end times of meetings currently running.
For each meeting, pop every heap top that is less than or equal to its start; those rooms freed.
Push the current meeting's end time onto the heap.
Update a running maximum of the heap size after each push.
Return that maximum, the peak number of simultaneously active meetings.
complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n)
pitfall: Counting a meeting that ends exactly when the next begins as an overlap, or returning the final heap size instead of its maximum.
bruteForce: Sweep every time unit in the range counting active meetings, O(n * T).

title: Graph Valid Tree
insight: A tree on n nodes is exactly n-1 edges with no cycle. Check the count first, then union every edge, and those two facts together force connectivity.
steps: Return false unless edges.length equals n - 1; that rules out forests and extra edges.
Initialise a parent array over n nodes, each its own root, plus a rank or size array.
For each edge, find both endpoints' roots using path compression.
If the two roots are equal there is a cycle, so return false; otherwise union them.
Return true; n-1 edges with no cycle forces exactly one connected component.
complexity: Time O(n + E * alpha(n)), space O(n)
pitfall: Verifying only connectivity or only acyclicity; you need both, and the n-1 edge count is what makes one check imply the other.
bruteForce: BFS from every node to check all others are reachable, plus a separate cycle hunt, O(n(n+E)).

title: Missing Number
insight: Every present value pairs with its own index under XOR and cancels, so XOR-ing 0 through n together with all array entries leaves exactly the missing number.
steps: Initialise result to n, the index that has no array slot of its own.
Loop i from 0 to n-1, XOR-ing result with i and then with nums[i].
Return result; every matched index-value pair has cancelled to 0.
As an alternative, compute n*(n+1)/2 and subtract the array sum.
Prefer XOR when overflow is a concern, since it never grows past the word size.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Looping i all the way to n and indexing nums[n], which is out of bounds; seed the result with n and let the loop cover only 0 to n-1.
bruteForce: Sort the array and scan for the first index where nums[i] is not i, O(n log n).

title: Alien Dictionary
pattern: Topological sort of a letter graph
insight: Only the first differing character of two adjacent words gives an ordering edge; everything after it says nothing, and a long word before its own prefix is a contradiction.
steps: Collect every distinct letter as a node, including letters with no constraints at all.
For each adjacent word pair, scan to the first differing char, add one edge, then stop.
If no char differs and the earlier word is longer, return the empty string.
Run Kahn's algorithm with indegrees over the letter nodes, appending each popped letter.
Return the built string only if it holds every distinct letter, else empty because of a cycle.
complexity: Time O(total chars + 26^2), space O(26^2)
pitfall: Adding edges at every position instead of only the first mismatch, or missing the invalid prefix case where abc precedes ab.
bruteForce: Try every permutation of the distinct letters and test the dictionary order, O(k! k).

title: Encode and Decode Strings
insight: Any delimiter you pick can also appear inside a payload, so prefix each string with its length; the decoder reads the length and then takes exactly that many characters.
steps: encode: for each string append its length as digits, then a hash sign, then the string.
decode: start at index 0 and read digits up to the next hash sign to get the length.
Slice the next length characters as one string and append it to the output list.
Advance the index past that slice and repeat until the input is consumed.
An empty string encodes as 0 then hash and round-trips; an empty list encodes as the empty string.
complexity: Time O(total chars) each way, space O(total chars)
pitfall: Joining on a separator character and splitting on it later, which corrupts any input string that itself contains that character.
bruteForce: Escape the delimiter inside each string and unescape on decode, O(total chars) with fiddly edge cases.

title: First Bad Version
insight: isBadVersion is monotone, false then true, so binary search the boundary keeping the invariant that the first bad version always lies inside [lo, hi].
steps: Set lo to 1 and hi to n.
While lo is less than hi, compute mid as lo + (hi - lo) / 2.
If isBadVersion(mid) is true, set hi to mid, since mid is still a candidate.
Otherwise set lo to mid + 1, since mid and everything before it is good.
Return lo once the range collapses; it is the first bad version.
complexity: Time O(log n) API calls, space O(1)
pitfall: Computing mid as (lo + hi) / 2, which overflows a 32-bit int when n approaches 2^31 - 1.
bruteForce: Call isBadVersion on 1, 2, 3 and so on until it returns true, O(n) API calls.

title: Walls and Gates
insight: BFS per room repeats work. Seed one queue with every gate at distance 0, and the first time BFS reaches a room that distance is already the minimum over all gates.
steps: Scan the whole grid and enqueue every cell equal to 0, which are the gates.
BFS level by level, or carry an explicit distance alongside each queued cell.
For each in-bounds neighbour whose value is INF (2147483647), set it to distance + 1 and enqueue.
Skip cells valued -1 (walls) and any already-assigned room; the INF test is the visited mark.
Mutate the grid in place and return nothing; rooms with no reachable gate keep INF.
complexity: Time O(m n), space O(m n) for the queue
pitfall: Running a separate search per empty room, or overwriting a room that already holds a smaller distance because INF was not used as the visited test.
bruteForce: BFS from every empty room out to its nearest gate, O((m n)^2).

title: Find the Duplicate Number
pattern: Floyd cycle detection on index map
insight: Read i to nums[i] as a functional graph. With n+1 slots holding values in [1, n], two indices point at the same node, so the cycle entrance is the repeated value.
steps: Walk slow one step and fast two steps through i to nums[i] until the two pointers meet.
Reset slow to index 0, which can never sit inside a cycle because every value is at least 1.
Advance slow and fast one step each until they meet again.
Return the index where they meet; it is the cycle entrance and therefore the duplicate value.
If mutation were allowed instead, negate nums[abs(v)] as a visited mark.
If reading is free but O(1) space is required, binary search the value range on count instead.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Assuming the duplicate appears exactly twice; it may appear many times, which breaks XOR and sum tricks but not cycle detection.
bruteForce: Sort or use a hash set, O(n log n) time or O(n) space, both ruled out by the constraints.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
pattern: Two heaps split at the median
insight: Split the stream at the median: a max-heap over the lower half and a min-heap over the upper half, sizes kept within one, put the median right at the heap tops.
steps: Keep lo as a max-heap and hi as a min-heap, with size(lo) equal to size(hi) or one more.
addNum: push onto lo, then immediately move lo's top across into hi.
If hi is now bigger than lo, move hi's top back into lo to restore the size invariant.
findMedian: return lo's top when sizes differ, else average the two tops.
Average the two tops in floating point; integer division would truncate a median of 1.5 to 1.
complexity: Time O(log n) per add, O(1) per median, space O(n)
pitfall: Rebalancing by size alone without pushing the value through the other heap, which lets an element get stranded in the wrong half.
bruteForce: Maintain a sorted list with binary-search insertion, O(n) per add from the shifting.

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
insight: Preorder plus an explicit marker for every null child is unambiguous, so deserialization is one left-to-right consume of tokens with no index arithmetic at all.
steps: serialize: preorder recursion appending the value, or a hash marker for null, comma separated.
Recurse left then right unconditionally so every missing child emits its own marker.
deserialize: split on commas and keep one shared mutable cursor into the token list.
Read one token; if it is the null marker return null, else build the node and recurse left then right.
Values can be negative, so parse signs; the empty tree serializes to just the null marker.
complexity: Time O(n) each way, space O(n)
pitfall: Omitting markers for null children, which makes preorder ambiguous, or passing the cursor by value so recursive calls lose progress.
bruteForce: Store preorder plus inorder and rebuild, O(n) but wrong once values repeat.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
insight: Keep tails[i] as the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length i+1. tails stays sorted, so each value replaces the first tail not smaller than it.
steps: Create an empty array tails.
For each x, binary search tails for the leftmost element greater than or equal to x.
If such a position exists, overwrite it with x, keeping that length reachable with a smaller tail.
If none exists, append x, extending the longest subsequence found so far by one.
Return tails.length; tails itself is not a valid subsequence, only its length is meaningful.
complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n)
pitfall: Using an upper bound rather than a lower bound in the search, which admits equal values and computes the longest non-decreasing run instead.
bruteForce: O(n^2) DP where dp[i] scans every j below i, or O(2^n) subset enumeration.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
insight: The cooldown is captured by one extra state: after selling you must pass through a rest day, so hold can only be entered from rest, never directly from sold.
steps: Track hold (own stock), sold (sold today), rest (free to buy) as running maxima.
Initialise hold to -prices[0], sold to negative infinity, rest to 0.
Each day compute newHold as max(hold, rest - price).
Compute newSold as hold + price and newRest as max(rest, sold).
Assign all three from the previous day's values at once, then advance to the next day.
Return max(sold, rest) at the end, since still holding stock is never optimal.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Updating the three states in place so a same-day value leaks into another transition, or letting hold come from sold and losing the cooldown day.
bruteForce: Recurse over buy, sell or skip at each day, O(2^n) without memoization.

title: Minimum Height Trees
pattern: Peel leaf layers to the centroids
insight: The best roots are the one or two centers of the tree, found by repeatedly stripping every current leaf. Whatever survives the final round is the whole answer.
steps: Return [0] when n is 1, since that lone node has no edges and never reaches degree 1.
Build adjacency lists and a degree array; collect all degree 1 nodes as the first leaf layer.
While more than 2 nodes remain, remove the entire current leaf layer at once.
Decrement each surviving neighbour's degree and gather those dropping to 1 as the next layer.
Subtract the removed count from the remaining total each round.
Return the 1 or 2 nodes left; a tree never has more than two centers.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n)
pitfall: Peeling one leaf at a time instead of a full layer, which breaks the symmetry, or missing the n equals 1 case entirely.
bruteForce: BFS from every node to measure its eccentricity and keep the minima, O(n^2).

title: Burst Balloons
pattern: Interval DP on the last burst
insight: Choosing which balloon bursts first makes subproblems interact. Ask instead which balloon in an open interval bursts last, because then its neighbours are the fixed boundaries.
steps: Pad nums with a 1 at each end so boundary multiplications need no special case.
Let dp[i][j] be the best score from bursting everything strictly between indices i and j.
Iterate interval length from 2 upward, and i left to right with j set to i + len.
For each k strictly between i and j, try dp[i][k] + nums[i]*nums[k]*nums[j] + dp[k][j].
Store the maximum into dp[i][j]; k is the balloon burst last within that interval.
Return dp[0][n+1] over the padded array.
complexity: Time O(n^3), space O(n^2)
pitfall: Framing the DP around the first burst, which splits the array into pieces that are no longer independent, making the recurrence wrong.
bruteForce: Try every possible bursting order, O(n!).

title: Coin Change
insight: Greedily taking the largest coin fails (coins 1, 3, 4 for amount 6), so build the minimum coin count for every amount up to the target out of smaller amounts.
steps: Create dp of size amount+1 filled with a sentinel such as amount+1, then set dp[0] to 0.
Loop a from 1 to amount, and inside it loop over every coin.
When coin is at most a, set dp[a] to min(dp[a], dp[a - coin] + 1).
Return -1 if dp[amount] still equals the sentinel, otherwise return dp[amount].
Amount 0 returns 0, and coins larger than the current amount are simply skipped.
complexity: Time O(amount * number of coins), space O(amount)
pitfall: Using greedy largest-coin-first, or filling dp with a true infinity that overflows when you add 1 to it.
bruteForce: Recurse over every coin choice at every step, O(coins^amount) without memoization.

title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
insight: Start the count at n and decrement only when a union actually merges two different roots. An edge inside an existing component changes nothing.
steps: Initialise parent and rank arrays over n nodes and a counter set to n.
For each edge, find the root of both endpoints using path compression.
If the two roots match, skip the edge; it is a redundant intra-component edge.
Otherwise attach the smaller tree under the larger and decrement the counter by 1.
Return the counter; isolated nodes with no edges are already included in it.
complexity: Time O(n + E * alpha(n)), space O(n)
pitfall: Decrementing the counter once per edge rather than only on a successful merge, which undercounts components whenever the graph has a cycle.
bruteForce: Build an adjacency matrix and DFS from each unvisited node, O(n^2).

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
pattern: Top-down DP with memo on cells
insight: Strictly increasing values mean a path can never revisit a cell, so the subproblem 'longest increasing path starting here' is acyclic and cacheable with no visited set.
steps: Allocate a memo matrix of zeros, where 0 means not yet computed.
Define dfs(r, c): return the memo value when non-zero, otherwise start best at 1.
For each of the four in-bounds neighbours with a strictly greater value, try 1 + dfs(neighbour).
Store the maximum into memo[r][c] and return it.
Run dfs from every cell and return the global maximum; a 1x1 grid correctly returns 1.
complexity: Time O(m n), space O(m n)
pitfall: Adding a backtracking visited set, which makes cached values path-dependent and wrong, or letting equal neighbours extend the path.
bruteForce: Plain DFS from every cell with no memo, exponential in the path length.

title: Reconstruct Itinerary
insight: The tickets form a graph with an Eulerian path from JFK. Visit destinations in sorted order but append an airport to the route only once its tickets are gone, then reverse.
steps: Group tickets by origin into a min-heap or sorted list of destinations per airport.
DFS from JFK, always consuming the smallest unused destination and removing that ticket.
When an airport has no outgoing tickets left, append it to a route list.
After the DFS fully unwinds, reverse the route list to get the itinerary.
The result holds tickets.length + 1 airports and uses every ticket exactly once.
complexity: Time O(E log E), space O(E) for E tickets
pitfall: Greedy DFS that appends airports on entry; a dead end then strands tickets, and the post-order append plus reverse is exactly what fixes it.
bruteForce: Backtrack over all ticket orderings and keep the smallest valid itinerary, O(E!).

title: Counting Bits
pattern: DP on i shifted right by one
insight: Dropping the last bit of i gives a smaller number already solved, so popcount(i) equals popcount(i >> 1) plus the low bit (i & 1).
steps: Allocate ans of length n+1 and set ans[0] to 0.
Loop i from 1 up to n inclusive.
Set ans[i] to ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1).
Return ans; n may be 0, for which the single-element array [0] is the right answer.
An equivalent recurrence is ans[i] = ans[i & (i-1)] + 1, clearing the lowest set bit.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the output
pitfall: Running a shift-and-count loop per number, which is O(n log n) and misses the whole point of the DP framing.
bruteForce: Count the bits of each i independently by shifting, O(n log n).

title: Top K Frequent Elements
insight: No frequency can exceed n, so index buckets by count and read them from the top down. That avoids any comparison sort of the counts.
steps: Count occurrences of each value into a hash map in one pass.
Create n+1 buckets and append each distinct value into the bucket for its count.
Walk the buckets from index n down to 1, collecting values as you go.
Stop as soon as k values have been collected and return them.
The answer is guaranteed unique, so ties across a bucket boundary cannot arise.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n)
pitfall: Sizing the bucket array by k instead of n, or heapifying all n counts for O(n log n) when a size-k heap or buckets is what is wanted.
bruteForce: Sort all distinct values by count, O(d log d) for d distinct values.

title: Design Twitter
pattern: Per-user tweet lists plus k-way merge
insight: Store each user's tweets newest-first with a global timestamp. The feed is then a k-way merge over the user's own list and their followees' lists, cut off after 10.
steps: Keep a global counter, a map user to list of (time, tweetId), and a map user to followee set.
postTweet: append (counter++, tweetId) to that user's own list.
getNewsFeed: take the user plus their followees and push each list's newest entry into a max-heap by time.
Pop up to 10 times, each time pushing the next older entry from the same user's list.
follow: add to the set, ignoring a self-follow; unfollow: discard, a no-op when absent.
A user's own tweets must appear even when they follow nobody.
complexity: Time O(f + 10 log f) per feed for f followees
pitfall: Scanning and sorting every tweet in the system on each feed call, or leaving the requesting user's own tweets out of the merge.
bruteForce: Gather all tweets from the user and followees and sort by time, O(T log T).

title: Sum of Two Integers
insight: XOR gives the sum with all carries ignored, and AND shifted left by one gives exactly those carries, so loop until no carry remains.
steps: Loop while b is non-zero.
Compute carry as (a & b) << 1.
Set a to a ^ b, then set b to carry.
Return a once b has become 0.
In languages with arbitrary-precision ints, mask with 0xFFFFFFFF each round and reinterpret as signed.
complexity: Time O(1), at most 32 iterations, space O(1)
pitfall: In Python the loop never terminates on negative inputs without a 32-bit mask plus a final two's-complement sign conversion.
bruteForce: Hand-roll a full adder over all 32 bit positions with explicit carry, same O(1) but far more code.

title: Ransom Note
insight: Magazine letters are consumable, so count what the magazine supplies and spend one per ransom-note letter, failing the instant a count would go negative.
steps: Return false when ransomNote is longer than magazine; a cheap early exit.
Count the 26 lowercase letters of magazine into an array.
Walk ransomNote, decrementing the counter for each character.
Return false as soon as any counter drops below zero.
Return true after the loop; every magazine letter was used at most once.
complexity: Time O(n + m), space O(1) for 26 counters
pitfall: Checking only that each note letter appears somewhere in the magazine, which ignores that a magazine letter cannot be reused.
bruteForce: For each note letter scan the magazine and delete the match, O(n m).

title: Longest Palindrome
insight: A palindrome uses every even count fully plus the even part of every odd count, and then one single leftover character in the middle if any odd count existed.
steps: Count every character; the alphabet is case sensitive, so A and a are different letters.
Sum count minus (count mod 2) across all characters, taking each count's even part.
Track separately whether any count was odd.
Add 1 to the total if at least one odd count existed, for the single center character.
Return the total; a one-character string gives 1 and all-even counts need no center.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) for a fixed alphabet
pitfall: Adding 1 for every odd count instead of just once overall, or folding case so that A and a get merged.
bruteForce: Test every subsequence for a palindromic rearrangement, O(2^n).

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
insight: Two equal halves exist exactly when some subset sums to total/2, so it is a reachability question over sums, not a search over subsets. An odd total is an instant false.
steps: Sum nums. If the sum is odd return false. Otherwise set target to sum/2.
Allocate a boolean array reach of size target+1 with reach[0] true and the rest false.
For each num, loop j from target down to num and set reach[j] = reach[j] or reach[j-num].
The descending inner loop is the invariant: reach[j-num] is still the previous item's row, so each num is used once.
Return reach[target].
complexity: Time O(n*sum/2), space O(sum/2); sum is at most 20000 here
pitfall: Looping j upward lets a single number be reused many times, silently solving unbounded knapsack and returning true for cases like [1,5].
bruteForce: Enumerate all 2^n subsets and test each sum against half the total: O(2^n).

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
insight: Searching forward from every cell repeats work. Invert the flow: start at the ocean edges and walk uphill to cells of height greater or equal, which marks every cell that can drain there.
steps: Make two boolean grids pac and atl, both all false.
DFS from every cell in row 0 and column 0 into pac; from the last row and last column into atl.
In the DFS move to a 4-neighbor only if it is in bounds, unvisited, and its height is >= the current cell's height.
Mark each visited cell in its own grid before recursing so a plateau of equal heights does not loop forever.
Collect and return every [r,c] where pac and atl are both true.
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(m*n) for the two visited grids
pitfall: Flipping the comparison to strictly greater breaks flat regions and equal-height border runs; the uphill test must allow equal heights.
bruteForce: Run a separate downhill DFS from each of the m*n cells and check if it reaches both oceans: O(m^2*n^2).

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
insight: A window is achievable when its length minus the count of its most frequent letter is at most k, because every other letter gets replaced. So track only that one number.
steps: Keep a 26-slot count array, left at 0, and maxCount as the largest count seen inside any window so far.
Move right across s, increment count[s[right]], and set maxCount = max(maxCount, count[s[right]]).
While (right - left + 1) - maxCount > k, decrement count[s[left]] and advance left.
Record answer = max(answer, right - left + 1) after each shrink.
Never shrink maxCount: a stale value only holds the window at its best past size, which cannot overstate the answer.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(26)
pitfall: People record the answer before shrinking, so an invalid window of width maxCount+k+1 gets counted once at every position it occurs.
bruteForce: Check every substring, counting letters to see if length minus the top count is at most k: O(n^2 * 26).

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
insight: Minimum removals equals total minus the largest non-overlapping set. Always keeping the interval that ends soonest leaves the most room for the rest, so earliest-end greedy is optimal.
steps: Sort intervals by end ascending.
Set lastEnd to the first interval's end and kept to 1.
For each later interval, if its start >= lastEnd then keep it: increment kept and set lastEnd to its end.
Otherwise it overlaps the kept one and is dropped; leave lastEnd alone since the kept interval ends no later.
Return intervals.length - kept.
complexity: Time O(n log n) for the sort, space O(1) beyond the sort
pitfall: Touching intervals are allowed here, so the test must be start >= lastEnd; using strict > removes [1,2] and [2,3] as a conflict.
bruteForce: DP over intervals sorted by start, checking every earlier interval for compatibility: O(n^2).

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
insight: An anagram is fully described by its letter counts, and the window length is fixed at len(p), so slide one window and update two counters instead of recounting.
steps: If len(p) > len(s) return an empty list. Build need[26] from p and have[26] from the first len(p) chars of s.
Track matches, the number of letters where need and have already agree, over all 26 letters.
If matches == 26 push index 0.
Slide right one: add s[i], drop s[i-len(p)], and after each single count change recheck that letter and fix matches.
Push i - len(p) + 1 whenever matches hits 26; return the index list.
complexity: Time O(n + m), n = len(s) and m = len(p); space O(26)
pitfall: Updating matches before applying the count change, or after both the add and the remove, desynchronizes the counter; adjust it once per individual letter change.
bruteForce: Sort or count every length-m substring of s and compare to p: O(n*m).

title: Target Sum
insight: Let P be the plus-signed set. Then sum(P) - (S - sum(P)) = target, so sum(P) = (S + target)/2. Counting sign assignments becomes counting subsets with one fixed sum.
steps: Compute S = sum(nums). If (S + target) is odd or abs(target) > S, return 0.
Set need = (S + target) / 2, a non-negative integer no larger than S.
Make ways[0..need] with ways[0] = 1 and the rest 0.
For each num, loop j from need down to num and do ways[j] += ways[j-num].
Return ways[need]. A num of 0 makes the loop double every entry, which correctly counts its two sign choices.
complexity: Time O(n*(S+target)/2), space O(S); S = sum(nums) <= 1000
pitfall: Forgetting that target can be negative, or skipping the parity and magnitude guards, lets (S+target)/2 land on a fraction or a negative index.
bruteForce: Recurse on both signs at every index: O(2^n) expression enumerations.

title: Coin Change II
insight: Combinations, not permutations, so you must fix a coin order. Putting the coin loop outside counts each multiset once, since a coin is only ever added after the coins before it.
steps: Make ways[0..amount] with ways[0] = 1 and the rest 0.
Loop over coins in the outer loop.
For each coin, loop j from coin up to amount and do ways[j] += ways[j-coin].
The ascending inner loop is deliberate: ways[j-coin] already includes this coin, which permits unlimited reuse.
Return ways[amount]; it is 0 when the amount is unreachable.
complexity: Time O(len(coins)*amount), space O(amount)
pitfall: Swapping the loops so amount is outer counts ordered sequences, so 1+2 and 2+1 both register and the answer is too large.
bruteForce: Recurse over coin counts at each denomination: exponential in amount/min(coin).

title: 01 Matrix
insight: Seed the queue with every zero at once. One BFS wave then expands from all zeros simultaneously, so the first time a cell is reached is its distance to the nearest zero.
steps: Create dist of the same shape, 0 at every zero cell and -1 at every one cell.
Push every zero cell's coordinates into a queue.
Pop a cell and for each in-bounds 4-neighbor with dist == -1, set dist to current+1 and push it.
The -1 marker doubles as the visited flag, so no cell is ever enqueued twice.
Return dist once the queue drains; the problem guarantees at least one zero, so nothing stays -1.
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(m*n) for dist and the queue
pitfall: Running a separate BFS per one-cell, or seeding from the ones instead of the zeros, turns a linear sweep into a quadratic one and times out.
bruteForce: For each cell, BFS or scan the whole grid for the closest zero: O((m*n)^2).

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
pattern: Post-order DFS with a global max
insight: The longest path has a single highest node, and there it is leftHeight + rightHeight edges. So compute heights bottom up and let every node try to be that apex.
steps: Keep a mutable best, initialized to 0.
Write height(node): return 0 if node is null.
Recurse to get l = height(left) and r = height(right).
Update best = max(best, l + r), which is the edge count of the path turning at this node.
Return 1 + max(l, r) as this node's height, and return best from the top-level call.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) recursion; h is the tree height, O(n) if skewed
pitfall: Returning l + r from the recursion instead of 1 + max(l, r) mixes up path length and height, so sibling branches get double counted.
bruteForce: At every node compute both subtree heights from scratch and take the max: O(n^2) on a skewed tree.

title: Permutation in String
insight: A permutation of s1 inside s2 is just a window of length len(s1) with identical letter counts, so one pass with a 26-slot counter settles it.
steps: If len(s1) > len(s2) return false. Build need[26] from s1 and have[26] from the first len(s1) chars of s2.
Set matches to the number of the 26 letters where need and have are already equal.
If matches == 26 return true.
Slide the window one step: add the entering char and remove the leaving char, updating matches after each single change.
Return true the moment matches reaches 26; return false after the last window.
complexity: Time O(n + m), n = len(s2) and m = len(s1); space O(26)
pitfall: Comparing the two 26-arrays element by element at every position is still accepted, but people often forget the empty-overlap guard when s1 is longer than s2.
bruteForce: Count letters in every length-m substring of s2 and compare: O(n*m).

title: Subtree of Another Tree
insight: A subtree must contain all descendants, so a candidate is pinned down by its root. Only test nodes whose value equals subRoot's value, then demand exact structural equality from there.
steps: isSame(a,b): both null is true; exactly one null or a.val != b.val is false; else isSame on both child pairs.
DFS over root. At a null node return false, since subRoot has at least one node.
If node.val == subRoot.val and isSame(node, subRoot), return true.
Otherwise return the DFS of node.left or the DFS of node.right.
For a linear bound, serialize both trees with null and delimiter markers and run KMP for a substring match.
complexity: Time O(m*n) worst case, m and n node counts; space O(m+n) stacks
pitfall: Comparing serializations without null markers and value delimiters produces false positives, for example tree 12 matching tree 2.
bruteForce: Compare subRoot against every node of root, O(m*n); that is also the standard answer here, and only the KMP route beats it at O(m+n).

title: Task Scheduler
insight: Only the most frequent task constrains the schedule. It carves maxFreq-1 blocks of width n+1, and every other task either fits in those idle slots or pads the timeline past them.
steps: Count each of the 26 labels and find maxFreq, the largest count.
Count how many labels tie at maxFreq, call it tied.
Compute framed = (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + tied, the length of the skeleton built around the hottest task.
Return max(framed, tasks.length).
The max matters: with many distinct tasks they fill every idle gap, so the answer is just the task count.
complexity: Time O(n) to count, space O(26)
pitfall: Returning framed alone overcounts whenever the leftover tasks already saturate the idle slots, for example many distinct labels with a small n.
bruteForce: Simulate interval by interval with a max-heap and a cooldown queue: O(total intervals * log 26).

title: Palindromic Substrings
insight: Every palindrome has exactly one center, either a character or a gap between two. Walk outward from each of the 2n-1 centers and each successful step is one more palindrome.
steps: Set total to 0.
For each index i, run an expansion with l = i, r = i for odd-length palindromes.
Run a second expansion with l = i, r = i+1 for even-length palindromes.
In each expansion, while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r], increment total, decrement l, increment r.
Return total; the invariant is that every counted (l,r) pair is a distinct palindromic substring.
complexity: Time O(n^2), space O(1)
pitfall: Running only the odd-center loop misses even-length palindromes like aa, so strings of repeated characters come out far too low.
bruteForce: Check all O(n^2) substrings for palindromicity by two-pointer scan: O(n^3).

title: Valid Parenthesis String
insight: You do not need to commit each star. Track the interval [lo,hi] of possible open-paren counts; the string is valid if that interval stays non-negative and can land on zero at the end.
steps: Set lo = 0 and hi = 0 and scan s left to right.
On '(' do lo++ and hi++; on ')' do lo-- and hi--; on '*' do lo-- and hi++.
If hi < 0 return false: even treating every star as '(' leaves an unmatched ')'.
Clamp lo = max(lo, 0), because a prefix cannot have negative open parens and stars absorb the slack.
After the scan return lo == 0.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Skipping the clamp on lo lets it drift negative and the final lo == 0 test then rejects valid strings such as (*).
bruteForce: Try all three meanings of each star and validate: O(3^k) for k stars.

title: Redundant Connection
insight: A tree plus one edge has exactly one cycle. Adding edges in input order, the first edge whose endpoints are already connected is the one that closes it, and processing in order makes it the last-occurring answer.
steps: Build parent[1..n] with parent[i] = i, plus rank or size for balancing.
Write find with path compression and union by rank.
Iterate edges in the given order.
If find(a) == find(b), return that edge: both endpoints already sit in one component so this edge is redundant.
Otherwise union them and continue; the problem guarantees exactly one such edge exists.
complexity: Time O(n * inverse Ackermann), effectively O(n); space O(n)
pitfall: Returning the first edge on a cycle found by DFS is not the same as the last redundant edge in input order; scanning edges in order is what satisfies the tiebreak.
bruteForce: Remove each edge in turn and test whether the remaining graph is a connected acyclic graph: O(n^2).

title: Max Area of Island
insight: Each land cell belongs to exactly one island, so one sweep that sinks every island it enters visits each cell once and the recursion itself can return the component size.
steps: Set best to 0 and scan every cell of grid.
On hitting a 1, call area(r,c) and update best = max(best, area).
In area(r,c), return 0 if out of bounds or grid[r][c] != 1.
Otherwise set grid[r][c] = 0 immediately, then return 1 plus area of the four neighbors.
Marking before recursing is the invariant that stops a cell being counted twice or recursing forever.
Return best; it stays 0 when the grid holds no land at all.
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(m*n) worst-case recursion depth
pitfall: Marking the cell visited after the recursive calls lets neighbors re-enter it, double counting area and risking stack overflow on a large island.
bruteForce: Repeated BFS from every land cell without a shared visited grid: O((m*n)^2).

title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
insight: You never need the whole stream, only the top k. Keep a min-heap capped at k and its root is the kth largest, so each add costs log k rather than a resort.
steps: In the constructor store k and build an empty min-heap, then add every element of nums through the same add path.
In add(val), push val onto the min-heap.
If the heap size now exceeds k, pop the root, which discards the smallest of the candidates.
Return the heap root, which is the kth largest once the heap holds k elements.
Heapifying nums and then popping down to size k is an equivalent faster init.
complexity: Init O(n log k), add O(log k), space O(k)
pitfall: Using a max-heap and popping k-1 times per query, or keeping the whole stream sorted, turns each add into O(n) and times out over 10^4 calls.
bruteForce: Store every value and sort on each add, reading index k-1 from the end: O(n log n) per query.

title: Binary Search
insight: The array is sorted and distinct, so comparing against the midpoint eliminates half the candidates. The whole trick is a loop invariant that keeps the target inside [lo,hi] if it exists at all.
steps: Set lo = 0 and hi = n - 1, an inclusive range.
While lo <= hi, compute mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 using integer division.
If nums[mid] == target return mid.
If nums[mid] < target set lo = mid + 1, else set hi = mid - 1.
Return -1 after the loop; lo > hi means the inclusive range is empty.
complexity: Time O(log n), space O(1)
pitfall: Writing while (lo < hi) with an inclusive hi skips the final single-element range and misses targets at the boundary.
bruteForce: Linear scan for the target: O(n), which violates the stated log-time requirement.

title: Accounts Merge
insight: Names are not identifiers, emails are. Treat each email as a node and union all emails listed in one account; the connected components are the people.
steps: For each account, union its first email with each of its other emails in a Union-Find keyed by the email string.
In the same pass record emailToName[email] = the account's name.
Walk every email, find its root, and append it to a map from root to email list.
Sort each group's email list lexicographically.
Emit one row per group: emailToName[root] followed by the sorted emails.
complexity: Time O(N log N) dominated by sorting, N = total emails; space O(N)
pitfall: Grouping by name merges distinct people who share a name; only a shared email may merge two accounts.
bruteForce: Repeatedly scan all pairs of accounts for a shared email and merge, until a pass changes nothing: O(A^2*N) per pass over A accounts.

title: Flood Fill
insight: The recursion stops on any pixel that is not the original color, so recoloring a pixel before recursing doubles as the visited mark. The one trap is when the new color equals the old.
steps: Read start = image[sr][sc]. If start == color, return image unchanged.
Call fill(sr,sc).
In fill(r,c), return if r or c is out of bounds or image[r][c] != start.
Set image[r][c] = color, then recurse on up, down, left, right.
Return image; only pixels 4-connected to the start through the original color were touched.
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(m*n) worst-case recursion depth
pitfall: Omitting the start == color guard makes the recursion never see a changed pixel and loop between neighbors until the stack blows.
bruteForce: Repeatedly sweep the grid recoloring any original-color pixel adjacent to a filled one until a pass changes nothing: O((m*n)^2).

title: Daily Temperatures
insight: A day is only waiting for the next strictly warmer day, so once a warmer day arrives it resolves every cooler day still pending. Keep those pending days in a stack of decreasing temperatures.
steps: Allocate answer of length n filled with 0 and an empty index stack.
For each i, while the stack is non-empty and day i is warmer than its top day, pop j and set answer[j] = i - j.
Push i onto the stack.
Invariant: stack temperatures are non-increasing bottom to top, so a pop resolves the nearest warmer day.
Indices left on the stack keep their 0, which is the required value for days with no warmer future day.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the stack
pitfall: Using >= in the pop test resolves a day against an equally warm one, but the problem demands strictly warmer.
bruteForce: For each day scan forward for the first warmer temperature: O(n^2).

title: Network Delay Time
insight: The time for all nodes to receive the signal is the maximum of the shortest-path distances from k. Weights are non-negative, so one Dijkstra run gives every distance.
steps: Build an adjacency list from times: adj[u] holds (v, w) pairs.
Initialize dist[1..n] to infinity, dist[k] = 0, and a min-heap holding (0, k).
Pop the smallest (d,u); skip it if d > dist[u], since that entry is stale.
For each (v,w) in adj[u], if d + w < dist[v] set dist[v] = d + w and push (dist[v], v).
Return max(dist[1..n]), or -1 if any node is still infinity.
complexity: Time O(E log V), space O(V + E); V = n nodes, E = len(times)
pitfall: Forgetting the -1 case for unreachable nodes, or summing the distances instead of taking their maximum.
bruteForce: Bellman-Ford relaxing all edges V-1 times: O(V*E).

title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
insight: The cost to stand on step i is cost[i] plus the cheaper of the two steps you could have come from, so only the last two values ever matter and the top is just past the last step.
steps: Set prev2 = cost[0] and prev1 = cost[1]; both are legal starting steps paid in full.
For i from 2 to n-1, compute cur = cost[i] + min(prev1, prev2).
Shift the window: prev2 = prev1 and prev1 = cur.
Return min(prev1, prev2), the cheaper of the last two steps, since from either you can step onto the top.
n is at least 2 by the constraints, so no empty or single-element case arises.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Returning prev1 alone is wrong: you can skip the last step entirely by stepping two from index n-2.
bruteForce: Recurse on one-step and two-step choices without memoizing: O(2^n).

title: Partition Labels
insight: A part cannot end before the last occurrence of any letter it contains. Precompute each letter's last index and cut the moment the sweep reaches the farthest last index seen.
steps: Make last[26] where last[c] is the final index of letter c in s.
Set start = 0 and end = 0 and walk i from 0 to n-1.
Set end = max(end, last[s[i]]), extending the current part to cover this letter fully.
When i == end, append end - start + 1 to the result and set start = i + 1.
Return the sizes; the invariant is that no letter in [start, end] appears after end.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(26)
pitfall: Cutting at the current letter's own last index rather than the running maximum splits parts too early, as in abab where a's last index is 2.
bruteForce: For each candidate cut point, check every letter on both sides for overlap: O(n^2 * 26).

title: Swim in Rising Water
insight: The time a path needs is the maximum elevation on it, not the sum. Run Dijkstra where a path's cost is that running maximum, so the first arrival at the corner is the minimum bottleneck.
steps: Push (grid[0][0], 0, 0) onto a min-heap and mark (0,0) visited.
Pop the smallest t with its cell; if that cell is (n-1, n-1) return t.
For each in-bounds unvisited 4-neighbor, mark it visited and push (max(t, grid[nr][nc]), nr, nc).
The max in the key is the whole trick: it propagates the worst cell crossed so far rather than a sum.
For n == 1 the start is the target, so the first pop returns grid[0][0].
complexity: Time O(n^2 log n), space O(n^2); grid is n x n
pitfall: Adding elevations instead of taking the running maximum, or marking cells visited only on pop without a stale check, both give wrong or slow results.
bruteForce: Try t = 0, then 1, then 2, BFS-ing the cells at or below t each time until the corner is reachable: O(n^4).

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
insight: At most k stops means at most k+1 edges, and one Bellman-Ford round relaxes exactly one more edge of path length. So k+1 rounds over a frozen snapshot bounds the hop count for free.
steps: Set dist[src] = 0 and every other dist to infinity.
Repeat k+1 times: copy dist into prev, then relax every flight against prev.
The relaxation is dist[v] = min(dist[v], prev[u] + w) for each flight (u,v,w) whose prev[u] is finite.
Relaxing from prev, not from the live dist, is what caps each round at one extra edge.
After the rounds, return dist[dst], or -1 if it is still infinity.
A Dijkstra variant also works if the heap key carries stops and a cell is revisited when reached with fewer stops.
complexity: Time O(k*E), space O(n); E = len(flights), n = cities
pitfall: Relaxing in place without the per-round snapshot lets one round chain several edges, so routes using more than k stops leak into the answer.
bruteForce: DFS every route from src with a depth cap of k+1 edges: exponential in k.

title: Hand of Straights
insight: The smallest remaining card has no smaller partner, so it must start a group. That forces the next groupSize-1 values, which makes the whole arrangement deterministic.
steps: If hand.length % groupSize != 0 return false.
Count card values into a map and sort the distinct values ascending.
Walk the sorted values. For value v with count c > 0, c groups must start at v.
For x from v to v+groupSize-1, require count[x] >= c then subtract c; return false if any falls short.
Return true after the walk; every card has been consumed by exactly one group.
complexity: Time O(n log n) for the sort, space O(n) for the counts
pitfall: Using the raw sorted array and advancing one card at a time instead of consuming count[v] groups at once makes this quadratic and easy to mis-decrement.
bruteForce: Try every partition of the multiset into groups of groupSize and test consecutiveness: exponential.

title: Car Fleet
insight: Work in arrival times, not positions. Scanning from the car nearest the target backwards, a car joins the fleet ahead whenever its unobstructed arrival time is no later than that fleet's.
steps: Pair each car as (position, speed) and sort descending by position, closest to target first.
Compute each car's free arrival time t = (target - position) / speed in floating point or as a fraction.
Keep a stack of fleet arrival times. If it is non-empty and t <= its top, this car is absorbed: push nothing.
Otherwise push t: this car is slower and forms a new fleet behind.
Return the stack size. Positions are distinct, so no tie in position needs breaking.
complexity: Time O(n log n) for the sort, space O(n)
pitfall: Comparing against the immediately previous car rather than the current stack top misses chained merges, and using strict < drops cars that catch up exactly at the target.
bruteForce: For each car, compare its arrival time with every car ahead of it to see whether any of them blocks it: O(n^2).

title: Koko Eating Bananas
insight: Feasibility is monotone: if speed k finishes in h hours then so does any larger k. So binary search the smallest feasible speed instead of reasoning about which piles to eat.
steps: Set lo = 1 and hi = max(piles); hi always works since each pile takes one hour.
While lo < hi, take mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 and compute hours = sum of ceil(p / mid) over piles.
If hours <= h set hi = mid, keeping the feasible candidate in range.
Else set lo = mid + 1.
Return lo. The invariant is that hi is always feasible and lo-1 never is, so they meet on the minimum.
complexity: Time O(n log max(piles)), space O(1); n = len(piles)
pitfall: Starting lo at 0 divides by zero, and using floor instead of ceil when counting hours understates the time because a partial hour still costs a full one.
bruteForce: Test k = 1, 2, 3, ... until one fits in h hours: O(n * max(piles)).

title: Middle of the Linked List
insight: Advance one pointer twice as fast as the other; when the fast one runs off the end the slow one is at the middle, and this loop variant naturally lands on the second middle for even lengths.
steps: Set slow = head and fast = head.
While fast is not null and fast.next is not null, advance slow by one and fast by two.
Return slow.
The invariant is that slow has taken half as many steps as fast, so slow sits at index floor(len/2).
For a single node the loop body never runs and head is returned, which is correct.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1)
pitfall: Looping on fast.next and fast.next.next instead returns the first of two middles, which this problem does not want.
bruteForce: Push every node pointer into an array and index element n/2: O(n) time but O(n) extra space instead of O(1).

title: K Closest Points to Origin
insight: Squared distance orders points identically to Euclidean distance, so skip the square root entirely and keep only the k best candidates in a max-heap keyed on that square.
steps: For each point compute d = x*x + y*y as an integer.
Push (d, point) onto a max-heap.
If the heap size exceeds k, pop the root, discarding the farthest candidate so far.
After the scan the heap holds exactly the k closest; return their points in any order.
For O(n) average time instead, quickselect on d to put the k smallest in the front partition.
complexity: Time O(n log k), space O(k); quickselect gives O(n) average
pitfall: Taking the square root adds floating-point ties for nothing; with coordinates up to 10^4 the squared distance stays under 2*10^8 and needs no big integer.
bruteForce: Sort all points by distance and take the first k: O(n log n).

title: Time Based Key-Value Store
insight: Timestamps for set are strictly increasing, so each key's list is already sorted by construction. A get is then a binary search for the rightmost timestamp not exceeding the query.
steps: Keep a hash map from key to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs.
set appends (timestamp, value) to that key's list, which stays sorted for free.
get looks up the key; if it is missing return the empty string.
Binary search the list with lo = 0 and hi = len-1 for the largest timestamp <= the query, tracking the best index found.
Return that index's value, or the empty string when every stored timestamp is larger than the query.
complexity: set O(1), get O(log m) for m values under that key; space O(total sets)
pitfall: Returning the nearest timestamp in either direction instead of strictly the largest one at or before the query, or forgetting the empty-string case.
bruteForce: Scan a key's whole list backwards for the first timestamp <= the query: O(m) per get.

title: Rotting Oranges
insight: Rot spreads from all rotten oranges at once, so a BFS seeded with every rotten cell has one level per minute. The answer is the number of levels, and leftover fresh oranges mean impossible.
steps: Scan the grid: push every 2-cell into a queue and count the 1-cells as fresh.
If fresh == 0 return 0, including the case of an empty or all-empty grid.
While the queue is non-empty and fresh > 0, process the whole current level, then increment minutes.
For each popped cell, any in-bounds 4-neighbor equal to 1 becomes 2, decrements fresh, and is pushed.
Return minutes if fresh == 0, else -1.
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(m*n) for the queue
pitfall: Incrementing minutes per cell rather than per level, or incrementing after a level that rotted nothing, overcounts by one; and the fresh == 0 start must return 0 not -1.
bruteForce: Sweep the whole grid once per minute, rotting neighbors, until no change: O(m*n*minutes).

title: Last Stone Weight
insight: The rule only ever needs the two heaviest stones, and the smash result is just another stone, so a max-heap gives exactly the access pattern the simulation asks for.
steps: Heapify all stones into a max-heap.
While the heap holds at least two stones, pop y then x, the two largest with y >= x.
If y != x, push y - x back onto the heap; if they are equal push nothing.
Repeat; each round removes at least one stone so the loop terminates.
Return the single remaining stone, or 0 if the heap is empty.
complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n)
pitfall: Forgetting the empty-heap case: when every stone cancels out the heap ends empty and the answer is 0, so reading the root directly is an error.
bruteForce: Rescan the array for the two maxima each round: O(n^2).

title: Longest Common Subsequence
insight: Compare the two last characters: if they match the LCS extends by one on both shortened strings, otherwise it is the better of dropping one character from either side. That recurrence is the whole problem.
steps: Let dp[i][j] be the LCS length of text1's first i chars and text2's first j chars, with row and column 0 all zeros.
For i from 1 to m and j from 1 to n: if text1[i-1] == text2[j-1] set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1.
Otherwise set dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
Return dp[m][n].
To use one row, keep prev and cur arrays of length n+1 and stash dp[i-1][j-1] before overwriting it.
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(min(m,n)) with the rolling row
pitfall: Mixing up subsequence with substring and resetting the length to 0 on a mismatch; a subsequence tolerates gaps so the max carries forward.
bruteForce: Enumerate every subsequence of one string and test membership in the other: O(2^m * n).

title: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling
pattern: DP over sorted ends plus binary search
insight: Sort by end time, then the best profit ending by time t is non-decreasing in t. Each job either is skipped or is taken on top of the best profit achievable at or before its start.
steps: Build triples (end, start, profit) and sort them by end ascending.
Keep arrays ends = [0] and best = [0], where best[i] is the max profit using jobs ending at or before ends[i].
For each job, binary search ends for the rightmost value <= its start and read that best value b.
Compute cand = b + profit and append this job's end to ends with max(best.back(), cand) to best.
Return best.back(). The arrays stay sorted and best stays non-decreasing, which is what makes the search valid.
complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n); n up to 5*10^4, times up to 10^9
pitfall: Times reach 10^9 so an array indexed by time is impossible; also a job starting exactly at another's end is compatible, so the search bound must be <= start.
bruteForce: Try taking or skipping each job with a compatibility check: O(2^n).

title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
insight: Goodness depends only on the maximum value seen from the root down to the node, so pass that single number down the recursion instead of inspecting the path again at every node.
steps: Write dfs(node, pathMax); return 0 if node is null.
Count 1 if node.val >= pathMax, else 0.
Compute newMax = max(pathMax, node.val).
Return that count plus dfs(node.left, newMax) plus dfs(node.right, newMax).
Start with dfs(root, root.val) or with negative infinity, so the root always counts as good.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) recursion; h is the height, O(n) if skewed
pitfall: Using strict > rather than >= excludes nodes tied with the path maximum, which the problem counts as good since no node on the path is greater.
bruteForce: For each node, re-walk the path from the root to it and take the max along the way: O(n*h), quadratic if skewed.

title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
pattern: Prim MST on a dense graph
insight: Every pair of points is an edge, so the graph is complete with n^2 edges. Dense Prim with an array of best-known distances beats heap-based approaches because the edge list is implicit.
steps: Keep minDist[i] for every point, set to infinity except minDist[0] = 0, plus an inTree boolean array.
Repeat n times: pick the unused point with smallest minDist, add its minDist to the total, mark it inTree.
For that chosen point u, loop over every point v not in the tree and set minDist[v] = min(minDist[v], manhattan(u, v)).
manhattan is abs(dx) + abs(dy); never compute or compare Euclidean distances here.
Return the accumulated total. A single point needs 0 edges, so the loop adds only the initial 0.
complexity: Time O(n^2), space O(n); n = number of points, up to 1000
pitfall: Forgetting the inTree check lets an already-added point be picked again with minDist 0, so the loop ends having connected fewer than n points.
bruteForce: Build all n^2 edges, sort them, and run Kruskal with Union-Find: O(n^2 log n).

title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
pattern: Offline sweep with a min-heap by size
insight: Answer the queries in increasing order. Then intervals only ever become available and expire, so a heap keyed by size whose top is lazily purged of expired intervals gives each answer in log time.
steps: Sort intervals by left ascending, and sort the query values while remembering each one's original index.
Walk the sorted queries with a pointer into intervals and an empty min-heap keyed by interval size.
For query q, push every interval with left <= q as (right - left + 1, right) and advance the pointer.
Pop while the heap is non-empty and the top's right < q: those intervals start early enough but already ended.
Record the top's size, or -1 on an empty heap, into answer[original index]; return answer.
complexity: Time O(n log n + q log q + q log n), space O(n + q)
pitfall: Writing answers in sorted-query order instead of back to the original indices, or popping by size without checking right, which discards a still-valid interval.
bruteForce: For each query scan every interval for containment and track the smallest: O(n*q), up to 10^10.

title: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet
insight: The operation only ever raises components, so any triplet with a component above the target is permanently poisonous and unusable. Among the rest, merging all of them is strictly best.
steps: Set bestA, bestB, bestC to 0.
For each triplet (a,b,c), skip it if a > target[0] or b > target[1] or c > target[2].
Otherwise update bestA = max(bestA, a), bestB = max(bestB, b), bestC = max(bestC, c).
Return true only if bestA, bestB, bestC equal target[0], target[1], target[2] respectively.
No triplet need supply more than one coordinate, and a usable one never hurts, so the maxima are independent.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(1); n = number of triplets
pitfall: Including a triplet that exceeds the target in any single component: merging it permanently overshoots that coordinate, since the operation can never lower a value.
bruteForce: Simulate merge sequences over subsets of triplets: exponential in n.

title: Detect Squares
insight: An axis-aligned square is pinned down by one diagonal pair. Fix the query point and try each stored point as its opposite corner; the other two corners are then forced, so just multiply their counts.
steps: Keep a map from (x,y) to how many times that point was added; add increments it so duplicates accumulate.
For count(x,y), set total to 0 and loop over the distinct stored points (px,py).
Skip unless px != x and abs(px - x) == abs(py - y): that is the diagonal test, and px != x forbids zero area.
The other corners are (x,py) and (px,y); add cnt[(px,py)] * cnt[(x,py)] * cnt[(px,y)] to total.
Return total. Multiplying the three counts is what honors duplicate points as distinct choices.
complexity: add O(1), count O(d) for d distinct points; space O(d), d <= 3000
pitfall: Dropping the px != x guard counts degenerate zero-area squares, and using a set rather than a count map undercounts when duplicate points were added.
bruteForce: Check every triple of stored points against the query for squareness: O(d^3) per count.
